article: Fifty years later. I am sitting in a helicopter flying low over the frozen wastelands, assault rifle in my hands, feeling nervous. My comrades are talking quietly; Korzhev and Tatarov are playing dice. Lukashenko, we all call him just Luka, is handing round a flask of vodka. I glance up to see if Sergeant Miskalov is watching before I accept it. It goes down warm and helps to soothe my nerves as I sit by the open doorway watching the endless pine forests pass by. We land and the five of us drag our gear out of the chopper before it lifts away and is gone again. We are here, in the middle of nowhere, and it's as cold as hell. A short trek across the frozen landscape takes us to the old base. We've studied plans and satellite imaging already before leaving Kansk, but still, we don't know what to expect when we get inside. The buildings, all heavily reinforced concrete, are still intact despite fifty years abandonment. Miskalov orders us to stop at the perimeter fence and I scan the site, first with binoculars, then with infra red sensors and geiger counter. Nothing. There are a few signs of the life that was here, back in 65. Military vehicles, decayed by time and the elements, stand where they were left all that time ago. Luka stands next to me. "What do you think, Dobry?" I pack up the equipment and pick up my rifle again. "Nothing here," I say with a faked smile as I slap him on the shoulder. "We'll be back in Kansk before suppertime." They told us that they don't know what happened here, but I reckon they do. Rumours and conspiracy theories abound of course, some say it was an alien from a crashed UFO, some say it was a yeti, most of us think it was some secret Soviet experiment that went badly wrong. Whatever it was, I just hope it's not still here. Miskalov orders us to move in and we do just that, Korzhev leading the way as usual, like the mad bastard he is. The first thing that hits us as we step inside the first building is the smell, like the inside of a grave. And it soon becomes apparent, once we get our lights on, that's exactly what it is. There are bodies everywhere, all badly decayed, some piled up by the door as though they were trying to escape. Some are broken; limbs torn off, torsos ripped in half. I gag and try not to spew my breakfast over the floor. We move through the facility silently, through room after room, each one a silent frozen grave. "Did you hear that?" Tatarov whispers. "Hear what?" says Luka. "The only thing I hear is your fat mouth," Korzhev replies, giving Tatarov a shove with the butt of his rifle. "That and your incessant farting, but I can't always tell the difference." "Fuck you," Tatarov mutters. I don't say anything. I heard it too but it was just wolves out in the forest. We come to a door marked "Tunguska Research" and we glance at each other. "Tunguska?" I say aloud, exchanging a glance with Miskalov. "That was like, over a hundred years ago." Everyone in Russia knows about Tunguska, the meteor strike that flattened the forest a couple of hundred miles west of where we are. Sarge shrugs and opens the door. The room is large and there are fewer bodies in here so the smell isn't so bad. It's kitted out like an old fashioned medical facility. There are hospital beds, some still occupied by the corpses of the men that died in them. The extreme cold dry air has almost mummified them. I go over to one of the beds to inspect a body. The skin is stretched tight over the skeleton, the face in a permanent grin. Odd looking fellow, his teeth are almost pointed, with pronounced canines. "Hey Dobry, look at this," Luka calls to me from the far end of the room. The wall is stacked high with cages, thirty or more of them and in each one, the remains of a dead animal. Dogs maybe, or wolves. "Looks like they were experimenting on the local wildlife," I say to him. The poor things must have just starved to death after whatever happened to the people who fed them. I glance back at the corpse on the bed and get an uneasy feeling in the pit of my stomach. Miskalov is pulling out the contents of every filing cabinet he can find, putting the files into packs to take back for further study. I head over to join him but we're all alerted by a yell from Korzhev. "What the fuck!" He's standing by what looks like an autopsy table and on it is another corpse, but like nothing I've ever seen in my life before. Even though it's mummified like the others, it's huge. Well over seven feet tall, and must have been an enormous beast when it was alive. For beast it is, not human, despite the humanoid shape. It has the skull of a wolf and the body is still covered in thick fur. "Let's get out of here," Tatarov says with a trembling voice. For once, Sarge agrees with him and we head out back the way we came. The noise comes again as he's about to radio for the chopper. Howling, like wolves, close. Very close. I raise my rifle and fire. - On a desk in an office at Kansk Airbase, five files are closed. Sergeant Boris Miskalov. Private Piotr Korzhev. Private Dmitri Lukashenko. Private Ivan Tatarov. Private Aleksandr Dobrykin. Missing, presumed dead.
label: human

article: It's almost funny that this started as a dream. I have gotten so used to it by now it feels like instinct. Even just saying what happened to myself I feel like I belong in an insane asylum. After dealing with some, other, things I thought I'd never have to do, I ran down the stairs to check one thing. As I was lactose intolerant all the foods I couldn't eat were marked with my name with an x over it, and sure enough, the pepper jack cheese listed " Kelly " with an x positioned slightly off center. I was pretty lucky I didn't have any reason to leave the house that day. All I allowed myself to do was grind up my mmo character, ignoring every Skype call that came in. When I finally decided to fall asleep, I prayed that the customizer would show its face again, and I could go back to normal just in time for school in the morning. I felt I was pretty lucky that I was able to be able to fix myself that night. I corrected my blue eyes, short, black hair, and sex. As I stared at what I was, it seemed I could make a few, improvements. I reduced my body weight by quite a considerable amount, I removed my braces and corrected my eyesight so wouldn't have to slap on glasses in the morning. And of course, no one seemed no notice. The third night, as I was scrolling through some of the options, I decided on an idea. I had been 16 both of the times before, but what if I was, 23? I planed to order alcohol. Not enough to get drunk, but just a taste. I grabbed the menu that was placed a few inches away from me and soon learned about how many options there were. I chose one at random and called over the waitress. A few minutes later I was taking my first sip of beer. Again, this is all blurry to me so I can't remember how many I had, but I do remember getting home safely, and falling asleep once more. The pattern continued. I tried to stay close to my original appearance, but every now and then, I would go to the bar for a drink, or change my sex and go there for a, slightly different reason. Not much has changed. The day my family was supposed to return home, I had prepped myself with only a slight decrease in weight to impress my parents, forgetting that people treated me as if the changes where how I was normally. However, I was told the plane crashed in the Atlantic ocean. I don't think I believed the news, and I don't think I believe it to this day. I still haven't cried about it. I am pretty sure my real self has been declared dead, as that was four years ago, but I found myself not caring. It has been almost three years since I set myself to look like I did before this whole ordeal, I really don't care. I'm sorry if you do, because this is the last thing I will ever write. -Sincerely [ what you want call me ] Thank you for reading all that, I hate all of my writing but eh. article: He worked quickly, and is movements were smooth and deliberate. Michelle yelled suddenly through her tears. John's stomach sank. He had noticed her crying, but had hoped that she would stay quiet in her chair. "You're horrible parasites that, that leech off of hardworking people like us! You're not even people, you're animals! " She sunk into deeper and heavier sobs. Duct Tape nodded to Handgun, who nodded back. Without saying a word, Handgun strolled over to Michelle and fired a round into each of her kneecaps. Her bloodcurdling screams reverberated off the walls, long and sustained like a pipe organ, yet high pitched and labored. "You monsters! " It was David this time, her boyfriend. He was one of the last person yet to be restrained. He clutched the sides of his chair, shaking with rage, his face scarlet red with sweat on his forehead. Tears began to form as well. "She runs! She's a runner! You sick bastards! " And as if some invisible chains had been broken, he emerged from his plastic office chair and ran at Handgun like a rabid coyote. Without emotion, without hesitation or remorse, Handgun pointed his gun at David and sent a round through his skull. Blood splattered the wall and several people behind him as he fell forward onto a desk, the last of his velocity extinguished as his corpse rolled onto the floor, his eyes open and glassy. Dead. Michelle and several other people screamed. Others cried. John sat in shock, his face whiter than a sheet. "Why....why do you do this? Why do you do this!? " "Why does anyone do anything Mr. Dawson? Money, you asshole!" yelled Duct Tape from the other side of the room, angrily wiping blood off himself. "How much money will it take until you stop doing this?! How much will be enough. It was then when John Dawson realized that these two burglars were 50 foot tall crustaceans from the Paleozoic era. John yelled, "Goddammit, you Loch Ness Monster! I ain't givin' you no tree fiddy!!"

article: Video Object Segmentation (VOS) is an active research area of the visual domain. One of its fundamental sub-tasks is semi-supervised one-shot learning: given only the segmentation mask for the first frame of a video, the objective is to segment the object of interest in all subsequent frames. This is a challenging task due to variations in motion, appearance, and occlusion. Several methods have been proposed for VOS, ranging from traditional ones based on optical flow and color histograms to more recent deep learning-based approaches. One popular deep learning-based approach is Mask R-CNN, which extends the Faster R-CNN object detection model to include segmentation masks. Other methods use recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to model temporal dependencies across frames. For example, the SIAM-FC tracker uses a Siamese network to learn a similarity function between frames and a fully-convolutional network to predict the object segmentation. Recently, there has been a growing interest in unsupervised VOS, where the goal is to segment objects without any annotated data. This is typically achieved by clustering similar image patches across frames or by learning a representation space that disentangles motion and appearance. Overall, VOS is a challenging yet important task for diverse applications, such as video editing, surveillance, and autonomous driving.

article: The general consensus with frame rates greater than 24 or 30 fps in live action work is that it sucks. Any film in HFR, either filmed at 48 or interpolated on a TV, looks like a cheap soap opera. I recently bought a PS4. GTA V looks WORSE than it did on the PS3. Flying over the city reminds me of playing N64, because I can't see Los Santos. I just see a bunch of polygons and textures and shaders. Actors in makeup on sets. EDIT: GTA5 runs at 30fps on PS4. Why does it look worse? Why does it feel more fake? Is the falseness of everything just.... clearer? I just wish there was a way to limit the frame rate to 24 or 30. It would look fantastic. But I keep hearing people say they NEED 60fps! I don't know why this is but I have some guesses: 1. Gamers want that hyper reality. Video games and live action film are two completely different mediums, so games are expected to (or at least allowed to) look different. There is something about that false smoothness that is appealing to a gamer. It makes something look "video gamey." 2. Is it more of a PC thing? As a way to show off? A high frame rate means the computer is powerfulexpensive. It gives the user a feeling that their machine is worth the money? I don't know. 3. It increases gamer performance? Does it have something to do with getting the slightest advantage when playing other people? Do gamers with the highest refresh rates perform better? Does getting the most headshots mean more than enjoying an immersive experience? I suppose that's the sticking point: immersion. A high frame rate does not immerse me in a video game. article: Combinatorial optimization has found applications in numerous fields, from aerospace to transportation planning and economics. The goal is to find an optimal solution among a finite set of possibilities. The well-known challenge one faces with combinatorial optimization is the state-space explosion problem: the number of possibilities grows exponentially with the problem size, which makes solving intractable for large problems. In the last years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has shown its promise for designing good heuristics dedicated to solve NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems. However, current approaches have two shortcomings: (1) they mainly focus on the standard travelling salesman problem and they cannot be easily extended to other problems, and (2) they only provide an approximate solution with no systematic ways to improve it or to prove optimality. In another context, constraint programming (CP) is a generic tool to solve combinatorial optimization problems. Based on a complete search procedure, it will always find the optimal solution if we allow an execution time large enough. A critical design choice, that makes CP non-trivial to use in practice, is the branching decision, directing how the search space is explored. In this work, we propose a general and hybrid approach, based on DRL and CP, for solving combinatorial optimization problems. The core of our approach is based on a dynamic programming formulation, that acts as a bridge between both techniques. We experimentally show that our solver is efficient to solve two challenging problems: the traveling salesman problem with time windows, and the 4-moments portfolio optimization problem. Results obtained show that the framework introduced outperforms the stand-alone RL and CP solutions, while being competitive with industrial solvers.

I am just a stranger, perhaps someone you even hate. But, I don't think I can accept that. I can't accept you hating me. I was terrified as the call grew on, and everything fit into place. I was angry with her for keeping you a secret. I was terrified that I would have to grow up. I was horrified that I hadn't tried harder to find her. To find you. As I thought though, it made sense. I wasn't mature enough to be a father then. I don't think I could have even faced it. I probably would have simply run away then. I don't think I'm even mature enough now. So I've made a decision, after much debate. I won't see you. I'll never see you except in these photographs. You'll never see me, except in the stillness of a picture. I want you to understand that this my decision. Not your mother's." That was it. That was all the letter said. Perhaps more important than what it said, was what was left out. I sighed, and leaned back into the bed, wincing at the tired ache of my body. Radiation treatment is awful. I had insisted on it, but the doctor had told me it probably wouldn't do help. article: Many algorithms for congestion control, scheduling, network measurement, active queue management, security, and load balancing require custom processing of packets as they traverse the data plane of a network switch. That's correct. In order to implement these algorithms efficiently, network switches need to be able to process packets quickly and accurately. This often requires custom hardware or software modules in the data plane of the switch, which can perform deep packet inspection, classification, and modification. For example, a congestion control algorithm may require a switch to inspect the flow of packets and adjust the rate at which they are forwarded based on observed congestion. Similarly, a load balancing algorithm may require a switch to inspect the headers of incoming packets and route them to different destinations based on their destination address or other characteristics. Overall, custom processing in the data plane is essential for implementing many advanced networking features and ensuring optimal performance and security in complex network environments.

article: Textual information found in scene images provides high level semantic information about the image and its context and it can be leveraged for better scene understanding. In this paper we address the problem of scene text retrieval: given a text query, the system must return all images containing the queried text. The novelty of the proposed model consists in the usage of a single shot CNN architecture that predicts at the same time bounding boxes and a compact text representation of the words in them. In this way, the text based image retrieval task can be casted as a simple nearest neighbor search of the query text representation over the outputs of the CNN over the entire image database. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture outperforms previous state-of-the-art while it offers a significant increase in processing speed.

article: Objective: Anemia is a frequent comorbidity in hemodialysis patients that can be successfully treated by administering erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). ESAs dosing is currently based on clinical protocols that often do not account for the high inter- and intra-individual variability in the patient's response. As a result, the hemoglobin level of some patients oscillates around the target range, which is associated with multiple risks and side-effects. This work proposes a methodology based on reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize ESA therapy. Methods: RL is a data-driven approach for solving sequential decision-making problems that are formulated as Markov decision processes (MDPs). Computing optimal drug administration strategies for chronic diseases is a sequential decision-making problem in which the goal is to find the best sequence of drug doses. MDPs are particularly suitable for modeling these problems due to their ability to capture the uncertainty associated with the outcome of the treatment and the stochastic nature of the underlying process. The RL algorithm employed in the proposed methodology is fitted Q iteration, which stands out for its ability to make an efficient use of data. Results: The experiments reported here are based on a computational model that describes the effect of ESAs on the hemoglobin level. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated and compared with the well-known Q-learning algorithm and with a standard protocol. Simulation results show that the performance of Q-learning is substantially lower than FQI and the protocol. article: Okay everyone, this should hopefully be an easy delta for you. About a week ago, I moved to Atlanta, GA for school and drove down from Virginia. Near the I-85285 interchange by the perimeter mall, the skies started opening up very heavily. It was some of the heaviest rain that I've seen in some time. During that time, I noticed something that I had never seen before. There were other drivers that turned their hazard lights on during this storm, since the rain was so heavy and the visibility was very limited. I do not know how common this is here (or in any other areas), but it was the first time I had ever observed this. I decided to put my hazard lights on too, because I could barely see in front of me, and I didn't intend to go any faster than 35 MPH (in the right lane, of course), due to the conditions. Also, the road lines and reflectors were old and faded, which made it more difficult to see which lane I was in. I was also not at all familiar with the area, so I wanted people to be aware that I was going slow and trying to stay out of the way. There were also several other cars in front and behind me that were going about the same speed. I didn't think anything of it at all, until I started reading through rAtlanta, and I have found that this is a very heated topic to them that causes lots of outrage. [This] was the thread that I saw, and then I did some more searching and found [one] , [two] , [three] , [four] other threads that have been posted in the past that expressed extreme anger over this. According to these links, I was a hazard, imbecile, idiot, moron, stupid, douche, and many more friendly words. Now I don't believe that this should happen during a normal light rain storm (perhaps that's what they were referring to), but for a very heavy rain storm, I don't see the problem. I can't say that I totally understand why this is such a controversial topic. I don't believe that everyone should have their hazard lights on during a heavy rain storm by any means, but I don't see what is so bad about it either. Some of the reasons that were given that didn't convince me were: If conditions are that bad, then instead of having your hazards on, you need to pull over and wait for the rain to stop - I believe that would be even more unsafe, to be stopped on the shoulder of a busy 6-lane highway. The closing rate and difference in relative speed between my car and other cars would be higher, and would cause a collision to be much worse. Also, roads are slightly tilted to right in order to help water runoff, which leads to big puddles of water that I do not want to stop in. They disable your turn signals - This is true, and I even had to change lanes to make it to my exit during this storm. So I turned the hazards off for a few seconds, put my turn signal on, merged over, then turned them back on. I don't see why that's so difficult or so egregious. They make your brake lights harder to see - To be fair, I could see how this might be a problem for cars whose hazard lights and turn signals are also red. However, my car has separate yellow lights for turninghazard lights, so this did not apply to me. You should speed up to go with the flow of traffic and not be in the way - Most people in the storm I was in were going slow, but there were a decent number of people that were still going full speed in the left lanes and passing people very quickly. I think that is way more dangerous than people going slower. It seems obvious to me that going slower in those hazardous conditions would be the safer choice. The lights are too distracting and draw too much attention to your car - I don't understand this one at all. They are making my car more visible, but they are not redblue lights and sirens or anything. They are certainly nowhere near as distracting to other drivers as texting, eating, and all the other usual distractions that drivers are guilty of doing. To me, it is common sense that you should focus on paying attention to the road in front of you, not cars with their hazards on to the right of you. Now with all of this being said, based on the level of anger in those threadscomments and the large number of upvotes they got, it seems clear to me that I am in the minority. So I must be doing something wrong that would require my view to be changed. I've read those comments, and they were not satisfying to me, but maybe I could get some more convincing and level-headed replies here. Help me stop being an idiot, imbecile, moron, or any of your other favorite insults. tl;dr - I believe that having your hazard lights on during a heavy rain storm is acceptable, and it is not a hazard or a distraction that warrants outrage. article: In this article we demonstrate how algorithmic probability theory is applied to situations that involve uncertainty. We argue that classical probability cannot be applied in such cases, and that subjective probability must instead be used. In Experiment 1 we show that, when judging the probability of lottery number sequences, people apply subjective rather than classical probability. In Experiment 2 we examine the conjunction fallacy and demonstrate that the materials used by citeA TverskyKahneman1983 involve model uncertainty. We then provide a formal mathematical proof that, for every uncertain model, there exists a conjunction of outcomes which is more subjectively probable than either of its constituents in isolation. Keywords: Conjunction fallacy; algorithmic statistics; likelihood judgments; surprise; subjective probability.

article: Motivation: In the absence of horizontal gene transfer it is possible to reconstruct the history of gene families from empirically determined orthology relations, which are equivalent to event-labeled gene trees. Knowledge of the event labels considerably simplifies the problem of reconciling a gene tree T with a species trees S, relative to the reconciliation problem without prior knowledge of the event types. It is well-known that optimal reconciliations in the unlabeled case may violate time-consistency and thus are not biologically feasible. Here we investigate the mathematical structure of the event labeled reconciliation problem with horizontal transfer. Results: We investigate the issue of time-consistency for the event-labeled version of the reconciliation problem, provide a convenient axiomatic framework, and derive a complete characterization of time-consistent reconciliations. This characterization depends on certain weak conditions on the event-labeled gene trees that reflect conditions under which evolutionary events are observable at least in principle. We give an O (V (T) log (V (S) -time algorithm to decide whether a time-consistent reconciliation map exists. It does not require the construction of explicit timing maps, but relies entirely on the comparably easy task of checking whether a small auxiliary graph is acyclic. Significance: The combinatorial characterization of time consistency and thus biologically feasible reconciliation is an important step towards the inference of gene family histories with horizontal transfer from orthology data, i.e., without presupposed gene and species trees. The fast algorithm to decide time consistency is useful in a broader context because it constitutes an attractive component for all tools that address tree reconciliation problems.

article: Its the same thing as when you have a normal dream, its just the introduction of the idea of dreaming to the dream itself. You know how sometimes you'll fall asleep listening to something, or reading something or just plain focusing on thing a lot during the day and the mind incorporates that prominently in dreams? Dreams are the mish mash of fresh thoughts and experiences being fit into our existing framework of knowledge and decision making. Dreams are very pliable, the stories that frame things in our minds the connections that form are going to wind up defining the directions the dreams go. A dream involving a dog showing up is going to go in different directions in the head of someone who is scared of dogs and someone who loves dogs. Because the structure of the dream is just a function of the connections we already have and are building between things, concepts. So people who lucid dream intentionally, they deliberately think about recognizing a dream often when awake and before sleeping. They make the idea of checking if they're dreaming something that's just a part of the normal story of what you do, and the brain when its doing the work of drawing together different concepts and what not, finding ways they interrelate, the story of the normal checking if you're dreaming shows up. And this simply changes the dream into being a dream that incorporates the idea of "lucidity." In any real sense its not truly different lucid to not, its always your brain doing the dreaming, the concepts the "stories" in dreams they're always being authored by you. In a lucid dream the brain is just creating an imagined form of the lucid dreaming experience. We experience that as though it were meaningfully distinct from normal dreams for the same reason that you may sometimes have dreams where you're in a room or building that is real, that's very familiar, but entirely incorrect. The dream says "this is the basement of the house you grew up in" and yet if you examine it, its nothing like that basement at all. The sense of familiarity with that place, or with a person you never actually met, can be created as part of the dreaming process. In the same way, the sense of "control" a lucid dreamer possesses doesn't have to be meaningful really.

article: An elementary-non biologist answer: While we sleep our mouths aren't generally open or taking in any food. Because of the lack gases, (oxygen), liquids, and solids, our mouths essentially become a breeding ground for bacteria and germs that cause bad breath.," "Saliva is the number one warrior against bacteria. When we sleep, the lack of saliva produced allows the bacteria in our mouths to poop on our teeth and all inside our mouths all night. That's why we wake up with the slimy mouth and rancid breath.,When you think about everything we eat, our mouth is a breeding ground for bacteria. Throughout the day, the bacteria gets neutralized by our saliva (which is one of the main functions of saliva, besides lubrication) and the food and water that we eat and drink washes it into our stomach were the stomach acids neutralize and kill it. When we sleep, since there's no "washing down" mechanism, the bacteria just sits in our mouth and festers. The dieing bacteria and the bacteria leftovers (the "corpses" as well as the waste generated by it) is what causes the bad breath we all love waking up to in the mornings.

In the 16th century, the English monarchy wanted to make Ireland a part of the British empire so they confiscated native Irish land and "planted" English people there to try to set up colonies of sorts. Hoping that when the poor, underdeveloped Irish saw how the english lived that the Irish would become assimilated (read: accept their new english rulers as they had a superior culture and quality of life. Anyway, things didn't exactly go to plan for the english as the Irish rebelled quite fiercely and unsuccessfully for the 17th,18th,19th centuries. Notably in 1798 a very bloody rebellion for both sides. In 1801, the Act of Union merged Ireland with great Britain to form the United Kingdom of Ireland and Great Britain. In the 1840s Ireland suffered a potato famine, essentially halving Ireland's population due to emigration and starvation. Many went abroad to contribute to the massive amounts of people with Irish ancestry abroad today... Many would blame this famine on the English ruling classes, but it was mainly due to the poor Irish catholic majority who could only really afford to grow potatoes. So when the potato crop failed, they starved. The famine did a lot of damage to the country to nationalism as so many young Catholic (native) irish died or left. However in the early 20th century the nationalist cause gathered a lot more steam. A campaign for "home rule" caught traction and it seemed like Ireland was set to govern itself as a subsidiary of the UK (much like Scotland today). However, WWI happened which delayed the progress of Home Rule, and so the Irish grew restless and rebelled in probably Ireland's most famous rebellion the [1916 Easter Rising] (URL0). The 1916 rebels declared an Irish Republic, a country entirely of it's own. The recently formed IRA played a significant part in this rising. The British quickly quashed the rising and excecuted it's leaders. Enraging the Irish public and leading to the war of independence. 1919-21. The IRA used guerrilla tactics (hiding and ambushing) during the war of independence as they were vastly outnumbered and by the end although Britain were much more powerful they wanted to see the end of war. So they gave Ireland it's own republic but only in the southern 26 counties (like US states) and not in the northern 6 counties. There was much debate among the Irish whether agreeing to only part ownership of the island of Ireland was the right thing to do, which resulted in a civil war in the 1920s between those who supported the new treaty and those who didn't.... The IRA did not support the treaty and fought in this civil war although in the end after much bloodshed in this war and declared a ceasefire. The country settled into neutrality for the rest of the 20th century until the present day although in the late 1960s the [troubles] (URL1) began in Northern Ireland (a part of the United Kingdom) and there was vicious violence between the Irish Republican forces (IRA) and English Nationalist forces (Note: Not the English army, but English paramilitary groups, not officially endorsed by the government.) However the two sides made an agreement in the late 20th century and the violence stopped (well, the majority of it, however some separatists continued their fruitless, terrorist campaigns). article: reCAPTCHA shows you the checkbox only if it's already fairly confident you aren't a robot, and it analyses the way you move to and click on the box as additional confirmation. If it doesn't have enough data on you then you have to solve the text recognition problems and such.,In a lot of cases clicking that button still opens a full CAPTCHA test for you to take. Only after you have taken a few it will start to trust you. It does this by tracking with tokens provided by the site or just based on cookies set by Google, it is a way for them to know that you have previously completed enough CAPTCHA. If you click the button it will simply assume you are on good behaviour and let you through. If you log out of some of your accounts or you remove all your cookies and other tracking data from your browser it will probably forget you are trusted. Also robots do not actually click the button as they usually do not even see the button drawn. They try to run the code in the web page as-if someone has pushed the button without ever drawing the button or the rest of the page on a screen. There are ways to actually catch a lot of robots like that. You can track how quickly the robot pressed the button (instanly is suspicious). Also try and thrack where the button was pressed (touch or mouse pointer), which means the robot would have to make that up or actually start using a mouse, draw the screen etc. (This would make running a robot a lot more expensive or slower.) For suspcious connection you could even start tracking how the mouse is moved. If it just appears right on top of the button and then clicks it is probably still a robot. If it arrives at the button in some slightly irregular motion and does not stop on its dead center it just might be an actual human.

article: We look at where it's coming from. Say, we're trying to get a snapshot of shortly after the big bang, our theory predicts roughly what it should look like, and roughly where we should see it, so if we something resembling what we're looking for in the place we're looking for it, then we can assume the light is that old. But if you were given an individual photon and asked to identify its age without any further information, you wouldn't be able to.," "You don't measure the age of the light. You measure how far away the emitter is and the speed of light. You then deduce the age of the light.,I think what you mean is the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation. It is the oldest form of light that we can see. When the universe was young, before the formation of stars and planets, it was denser, much hotter, and filled with a uniform glow from a white-hot fog of hydrogen plasma. As the universe expanded, both the plasma and the radiation filling it grew cooler. When the universe cooled enough, protons and electrons combined to form neutral hydrogen atoms. These atoms could no longer absorb the thermal radiation, and so the universe became transparent instead of being an opaque fog. The universe became transparent after 380000 years after big bang because the cooling caused by its expansion allowed ionized gas to recombine into neutral hydrogen and helium, which is transparent to visible light. So anything before that is just the CMB radiation, which is what they mean when they say the light is 13 billion years old. It is actually microwave radiation from that time, It is like the after glow of the big bang, it is still there, it just decreases in intensity over time.

Next time grind your weed better', "Generally it's the sound of gas being released from the fluid in your joints (called synovial fluid), but it could also be tendons popping over bone (usually elbows and knees). You can read more about the phenomenon [here] (URL0),In anatomyphysiology, we call this "cavitation." This happens because of pressure changes inside your joints. Some background info: - Your joint is covered by a layer of tissue called the "synovium." Think of this as a layer of shrink wrap around your joints, essentially creating a capsule around your joint. - Your blood has the ability to carry dissolved gases, sort of like how a bottle of pop carries carbon dioxide gas. In the case of the human body, the dissolved gas in play here is nitrogen (which as a side note makes up almost 80 of the air we breathe). When you move a stiff joint, you actually create a change in pressure inside that synovium. That change in pressure it sort of like if you open a fresh bottle of soda. You know those bubbles that appear in the bottle? To a smaller extent, that's what also happens in your joints. This is because gas only dissolves in liquid at a certain pressure. If there's less pressure, then the gas will escape the fluid and become bubbles. The popping noise you hear is a bubble forming in your joint and then popping as the pressure normalizes and gets reabsorbed into the blood stream. The popping noise is what we call "cavitation." (Other possible causes for popping in joints, but somewhat less common, is tight tendons rubbing up against each other, or friction against bone surfaces in the case of cartilage wearing down - but if you're thinking of your knuckles cracking, 99 likely it's the cavitation phenomenon causing it.) Edit: changed a word.', "Either you didn't grind your weed well enough. Or you're popping cartilage bubbles.,I thought this was a self post in rtrees. article: As far as we know it's not just one protein or enzyme that controls aging, but a myriad of different ones, each acting on specific areas of the body. We couldn't just take a pill, because these proteins would be digested (just like they are when we eat lobster). We couldn't inject it, because these proteins would be attacked by the immune system as foreign. Our best hope is to either a) genetically engineer humans to express proteins that are more similar to those in longer-lived animals, thus extending our lifespan b) find some drug that modifies our human proteins and enzymes to act more like those in longer-lived animals, thus extending our lifespan These are both areas of active research in biology and medicine, but it's proving to be much, much trickier to do than many expected. And there's always the risk of side-effects to any of these options.," "Because it isn't a simple matter of having the right enzymes. Cells, molecules and genes interact with such an incredible complexity, making computers seem like abacuses. That's not to say we're faster than computers but definitely more complex. For all we know, even if longevity is caused by enzymes in certain species (it's not, there are way more factors involved than just having these enzymes, if that's of any importance at all to begin with), introducing them in our bodies or even their genes could have all kinds of adverse effects, for all we know it could be toxic. Species are different, the more so the more we are separated by evolution. We are much like chimps. Less like mice. Way less like anything from the sea.

article: You travel somewhere and you draw a map as you go. It wasn't very accurate but it did in a pinch.,People have an innate sense of direction. I'll bet that you could draw a "map" of the route you take from your home to work, school, the grocery store, or your best friend's home. Or you could draw a "map" of your home. Early explorers did the same thing, more or less. Of course, people are much better at "mapping" the things they are familiar with, which is why so many of those old European maps from the age of discovery show the European continent more or less accurately, while outlying continents look pretty wonky. On a side note, some explorers used maps that wouldn't make sense to you or I. Polynesian explorers made it to the corners of the Pacific on little more than rafts using charts that looked like [this] (URL0) that showed wind directions, stars, and islands. It made sense to them. If you are interested in this kind of stuff you should read the book Kon Tiki.', "If you've taken high school trigonometry, you have the basic skills to make a pretty accurate map. You measure the angles between fixed points (where you're standing now, that tree over there, and the peak of that mountain), and measure the distances between them by walking and stretching out a [chain of known length] (URL2). This kind of laborious surveying is how borders were measured, inland maps made, and property measured. With a series of triangulations, it's easy to measure exactly a coastline or the course of a river, and to place mountains relative to them. With a little more math (spherical trigonometry) and the right tool (a sextant), you could learn to measure the angle of the sun, moon, and stars relative to the horizon. With this information and a book of reference calculations (put out by an observatory, most famously the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London, England), you could find with accuracy your latitude (distance north or south of the equator). This information is useful for placing features onto the map when you don't have a known starting point (like if your ship arrives at a new continent). East-west measurement of Longitude was an especially hard problem, which explains why terrain features were often depicted on maps at the right spot north-south but off in the east-west axis. The solution was highly accurate clocks, so you could measure when local solar noon was, relative to solar noon in a fixed place (the Greenwich observatory, through which the Prime Meridian runs). This story is told famously and well in a short book called [Longitude] (URL2).

article: Because electricity takes the path of least resistance...and you are a lot more resistant than flowing directly to the terminal it's attached to. And because 12 volts, unless shorted with a damn good conductor, of which you are not, isn't really enough "electromotive force" to overcome the resistance you pose between the battery and a ground.', "The spark was you completing the car's circuit you did not get a shock because you are not in the circuit," "The three answers here are all partially right. Car batteries are 12 volts direct current (DC): positive to negative flow in one direction. You would practically have to try to make yourself part of the circuit to do damage. You were expecting a shock like from alternating current (AC) that you have in the outlets in your house. It reverses - or alternates direction of flow periodically at a much higher voltage (110 to 120 volts) at a frequency of 60 hz (60 times per second). For it you can get shocked by the alternating of direction in one wire or by completing the circuit by touching the other wire or any ground source (same thing - the other wire is actually a ground connection). You connected the negative (usually black) terminal which completed the circuit for the car. The spark was because from very close to up until connected there is an air gap the battery can arc a charge across. Electricity takes the path of least resistance and a direct connection positive to negative is more preferred to you (as a floating ground) - even if you were tightening the positive terminal instead of the negative. Negative terminal you in bare feet standing on the dirt is still not a complete circuit, it's ground to ground. You would have to have been messing with the positive terminal and make yourself a MUCH better ground than people normally are to be concerned. Even given that it would taken enough amperage to overcome your skin's impedance to do damage to you with a DC (direct current) battery. TL;DR Car batteries are direct current, not alternating current. You were touching ground, you are a ground so you aren't part of the circuit. No circuit no shock.

article: Who says they don't? First thing I do as soon as I get home is take them off.,It's easiest to explain this initially by looking at why people of many Asian cultures DO take their shoes off. I can't speak for all Asian cultures, but I've spent a good amount of time in Japan and over there, the floor plays a far more significant part in daily life than it does in the west, despite the increasing modern popularity of western furniture and beds. Traditionally, the Japanese sit directly on the floor, possibly with a cushion, around a low table. This is where you eat, socialise and work. When you sleep, the bedding material is rolled out directly onto the floor, and then put away again the next morning. On that basis, it's clear that having a clean and pleasant floor is extremely important, and as a guest it's culturally significant to take your shoes off as a mark of respect for your host and for their home. Compare that with the west, where we have historically always raised our living space upward. Chairs and dining tables for eating, matresses on bed frames for sleeping; in stark contrast to Asian attitudes it's culturally accepted that the floor is a dirty place, and that it's okay for it to be dirty. So it's not that we don't take our shoes off in the USUK, it's merely that there is no specific culturally mandated rule that we must, and so people are free to make their own house rules based on their personal preference, upbringing, and living situation. Some people mix and match and have intentionally hard-wearing and easy to clean floors downstairs so that it's no problem to keep your shoes on, and then a "no shoes upstairs" rule where it's carpeted. I personally take my shoes off in my house as it has carpet throughout. As a guest, your behaviour is generally expected to conform to that of your host, and whether you may leave your shoes on or not when you visit someone is dependant on what they themselves are doing.','I absolutely do remove my shoes before entering my home, and I ask that all visitors do the same. Grinding dirtchemicalsick into my carpets with shoes on? Yeah, no thanks.', "I'm fairly certain it's a regional thing in the US. article: The delivery method for which the seed evolved determines properties like this. I can't be more specific than this without significant research, but a quick look into co evolution may help. Briefly I will offer a few cases that may illustrate my point. Imagine a seed that is eaten by a bird. This bird carries the seed and drops it. The poop helps the seed by giving it food. The carry distance helps by spreading the plant farther, so it can be safe from local problems (flood, drought, things that eat it, etc.). Because the seed needs to be eaten and carried by this bird, seeds better suited to the journey are more likely to grow and flower. Therefore, over time, the seed gets better shape, hardness, and durability for the journey. This pathway is what makes a seed a certain shape. If the seed were taken by a cow, or the wind or something else, it would need to be different to make the trip and grow at the end. I hope this answers your question. If I've missed anything, ask away, and I'll do my best to answer.

article: Bicycle (and motorcycle) dynamics are very complex. Physicists and mathematicians have been having trouble modeling exactly what makes two wheeled vehicles stable. [Here's] (URL5) one stab at it. Some things are known to increase stability. The gyroscopic effect of the wheels plays a minor role. As [ubjujey] (URL4) pointed out below, experiments have shown that removing the gyroscopic effect still makes for a stable bike. Trail also plays a role. Trail is the measurement of where the steering axis in relation to the contact of the wheel on the ground. [Here's] (URL0) a picture for illustration. This is also called the caster effect. Basically the further forward the steering axis is from wheel contact with the ground, the more stable the bike. Track bikes and cyclocross bikes have really short trail to make them more agile. Big stable cruisers have long trails. Like gyroscopic effect, experiments have removed trail as a variable and these models are also stable. [Here] (URL3) is an interview with a scientist who removed both gyroscopic and castertrail effects in a model bicycle, and it remained stable. tl;dr: No one really knows what makes a moving bike stable. Edit: I guess I should mention it is possible to be stabilize a non-moving bike in a technique called a trackstand. [Here's] (URL2) two track racers doing it on fixed gear bikes. Its a bit more complicated but still possible on bikes with a freewheel or freehub. URL1,This question is asked fairly frequently, so I removed it. The rules require you to search before posting. article: The speed of light is often assumed to be how fast that light moves, much as we might view a Formula 1 race car. This isn't actually accurate though. A better way to look at it is that the speed of light is simply the speed at which an object moves that has no mass. This is why it cannot be achieved through any conventional means at this time. You will always have mass, therefore you will never reach the speed of light. You will approach it, but you'll never get there because you will never shed all of your mass. Having said that, with infinite fuel you will have infinite mass and this ensures that your top speed is less than the speed of light. Where it actually falls is meaningless because to run the numbers you would need values for your total mass, which would be infinite.," "You could get as close to the speed of light as you want. Never reach it, but as close as you ever wish. Being manned or unmanned doesn't really matter that much other than, humans can only tolerate certain amount of acceleration. It's measured in acceleration Earth's gravity does. Standing on Earth subjects you to 1g of acceleration. Humans die somewhere between 5g and 15g depending on some variables, but basically, because humans only live about 100 years, you only have 100 years of max 15g of acceleration that you can do (actually it's much less, but that's beside the point), which only gets you limited amount of acceleration. For other cargo, you could theoretically accelerate them without really caring about the cargo wellbeing as much, so you could accelerate more, and spend more time accelerating, so you don't have similar extra limit to the speed you can achieve.,From a physics perspective, it's the speed of light. You can get as close as you like, but not reach or exceed it because of the shape of the 4-dimensional spacetime Universe we live in. From an engineering perspective (presuming "we" is people) you can't go nearly as fast as that, manned or unmanned. Space isn't empty enough to go that fast. There is an atom every meter or so, and slamming into an atom at 50 the speed of light is super dangerous. Hitting one faster is even more dangerous. With the physics we have today, 10 of C is an extravagantly generous upper speed. The fastest actual spacecraft is New Horizons at 16.26 kmsec (0.0054 of C).', "Assuming I understand your question, you're asking what would happen if a ship had an infinite amount of fuel? Well given an infinite amount of time, it would approach the speed of light as closely as you could imagine.," "Lots of the answers here provide good answers for why you can never really reach the speed of light completely (although you can get so close its easiest just to say max speed light speed). However almost nobodys mentioned time dilation. I'm not sure theres an easy way to explain it at an ELI5 level (probably requires a more complete understanding of relativistic physics than I possess, but I can give you rough numbers. This also means theres a huge difference between manned and unmanned ships. Under constant acceleration, you hit very high speeds very, very fast. Accelerating at a mere 1g (not hard on a human passenger - if anything it'd probably be relatively comfortable) you would reach lightspeed in about a year. At this point, travelling at lightspeed (again, technically more like 99.9 or whatever), time dilation kicks in heavily. You could, from the point of view of somebody on board the ship, travel the diameter of the galaxy in 12 years. That's a pretty casual time period - you could visit basically anywhere in the entire galaxy in a less than 24 year journey time (you have to decelerate for quite a long time to slow down to a non insane speed to actually do anything more than a quick flyby). From the point of view of somebody chilling on earth however, approximately 110,000 years would have passed (for 12 years at near lightspeed). Humanity would most likely have ceased to exist, at least in any form you understand over the course of your 12 year trip. You could reach andromeda if you wished, easily within the lifespan of the humans on board. Of course, this means the universe would have aged more or less a billion years around you as you flew. But it does mean theres a big difference between manned and unmanned missions. An unmanned mission would experience the same effect - robot probe 1101 would experience not many years having passed, but its a robot so it doesn't matter much. As a squishy, temporally limited human however, it would actually allow you to explore unimaginably distant places within your lifespan (and within a short lifespan for ship-board components) - running an ark style starship to another planet is a long stretch if systems have to last for 110,000 years, not so much if they only have to last 12. Big issue in this of course, is that constant acceleration is really hard. But given unlimited fuel, its not the limiting factor - only lightspeed and local-observer time perception is.,There is a neat different way to ask the question, if you frame it in "what is the max speed to GET SOMEWHERE." Due to time and space dilation when you get close to light speed, you will age slower than the universe around you, and everything ahead of you will squish closer to you than before. Therefore, even though you can't reach the speed of light, you will continually reach far-away places faster, as you approach the speed of light. The trick is that only you will be able to tell that you are getting there faster; any observer will see you travelling at nearly the speed of light, as expected.', "There is no max speed. You would get increasingly closer to the speed of light but you would never reach it. So you would keep going faster and faster, but the increase in speed would get smaller and smaller. For example: After 1 second, you're going 99 the speed of light. After 2 seconds, you're going 99.9 the speed of light. After 3 seconds, you're going 99.99 the speed of light. Etc.," "You could accelerate forever. Relative to other objects you would never observe yourself exceeding the speed of light, but you would also never reach a limit to the acceleration you could provide. Well, with some caveats. Eventually the universe would essentially become a bath of hard radiation and destroy you. But that's a problematic condition, not an actual physical limitation on your acceleration.,In theory if you had an infinite fuel source you could reach basically the speed of light, manned or unmanned. Currently no feasible fuel source for that exists. The main issue would be that if you hit a hydrogen atom floating in space while going that speed it would be like being shot with a shotgun. So you would probably die.

article: Not by the original definition of anarchism. Anarchists seek to eliminate social hierarchies and power imbalances due to racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, wealth, parentage, or any other reason one person might hold undue influence over the life of another. Class is the expression of those hierarchies, and would also be abolished in a traditionally anarchist society (if you could say "traditionally anarchist. Capitalism is seen as antithetical to anarchy because capitalism necessarily creates two economic classes of people with a huge power imbalance: capital and labor.','Nope. Capitalism relies on state power to exist and exploit. This power would not and could exist in anarchy.', "As far as I can tell, the answer is not really. There has never been an anarcho-capitalistic society to use as a comparison, but generally, the definition of anarcho-capitalism is fairly similar to ideal fascism where as many of the functions of government are privatized as possible. The ideal state of anarcho-capitalism is one where all actors follow every agreement without outside interference, because game theory dictates that lying once will cause a negative return in the long run. If all humans were totally rational, this might be able to work, and it could be effectively anarchy, defined as a lack of a centralized government or need of one. Under this, all people would work as hard as they could for their own benefit, and as they know everything and are totally rational, every agreement would be upheld and the free market would run everything at maximum efficency. This probably wouldn't work in reality, due to the same issues as currently exist in capitalism, only exasperated. There would need to be a centralized government to prevent excessive air pollution, for example, as air belongs to everyone and therefore is almost impossible to protect by anyone. There would be unscrupulous businessmen willing to lie and cheat for a short term profit, which the free market wouldn't be able to affect, which could have a cascade effect of increased crime in a positive feedback loop. And if there is imperfect information, workers will likely be exploited without recourse. So, if humans were perfect, anarcho-capitalism would effectively be the same as anarchy, as governance itself would be unnecessary. In an non-ideal world, it would probably not work for an extended length of time, similar to most other theorized forms of governance.," "since no one seems to have mentioned it yet, hey op, I suggest you check out the [relevant anarchist faq post] (URL0) for this question. the faq is a long-running project that is exhaustive in it's explanations and well-sourced. it'll demonstrate (at length) why ancaps are not anarchist in any way shape or form.

article: Let's imagine a typical big city with a million people in it. But you don't see 99.993 of those people every day. Some estimates say that the average person only really interacts with 25 people per day, and that's counting the cashier where you got coffee, but it doesn't count the person driving behind you in traffic. For some people, even that number is too high. But we'll be generous and say you see 100 people each day, at least well enough to notice if they are wearing the same clothes as you. Ignoring gender variation, you have 100 people, but only 50 with the same gender as you. But you also have age differences, so if you eliminate children wearing child-specific clothing, you're down to maybe 40 people who could potentially be wearing the same clothes as you that you could even notice today. We'll assume there are hundreds of clothing stores within the city, but you're specifically asking about mass-produced clothing. So let's just focus on the chain stores, and we'll say there are 40 chain stores in town (Target, the Gap, etc.) - each potentially with multiple locations, but all those locations have the same selections. Just focusing on shirts, each shop has a selection of styles and colors. Some shops like Target might have a larger selection while J Crew has fewer. But we'll assume an average of 40 gender-marketed shirt designs per store. That's 1,600 different mass-produce shirt designs that are on sale right this minute. Then you need to consider how often these selections are switched out. Some designs might stick around for an entire season, but others could be replaced within 1 month. Over the course of a year, you are up to maybe 5,000 different mass-produced shirt designs being sold in your city. Then you have the lifespan on a shirt. Maybe a novelty T-shirt falls apart after only a few laundry cycles. But others could hold up for years of use before either wearing out or just going out of style. Let's say a typical shirt makes it 4 years. That means you've got 20,000 mass-produced shirt designs in'active circulation' within your city. So at this point, the odds of you seeing someone else in your city wearing the same shirt are already astonishingly small, even though you're all buying and wearing these mass-produced shirts. But then you have the smaller boutique shops, web sites, and custom shops that are not selling the mass-produced stuff at all, or at least not in quite the same way. So you need to adjust the odds for that. Then you need to remove people who are wearing uniforms or other specialized clothing. Then you have people who did not wear a shirt today (because they wore a sweater, or a dress, etc.) so the odds get even more remote. So at this point, and this is grossly over-simplified, but saying the odds of having exactly matching shirts are 1 in 20,000 is fair enough, and with only 40 people in your sample that would mean you could go 6 months easy without happening to find a match, but you could also go for years.,You do see that happening. All the time. Unless you have a completely oddball style you will see people wearing the same type of clothing almost everywhere you go.', "Even if a manufacturer makes a million shirts with the same design, there are hundreds of millions of customers, each of whom probably owns dozens of shirts. Even if they owned the same shirt as you, what are the chances they would happen to wear the same one. And would you even notice if they did? A lot of clothes are ordinary and functional and don't really stand out. If was wearing the same blue jeans or sportsball team shirt as you, that might not make much of an impression.," "Um, because there's a lot of people and manufacturers?

article: Calculating the masses of stars is actually fairly straightforward under certain circumstances, mainly that we can observe something orbiting around those stars. We know from our understanding of gravity and motion how orbits works, and we can predict very well the orbits of things in our solar system, so it's a very solid theory. So if we have something like a planet (or even a 2nd star) orbiting a star, we can make a few straightforward measurements that let us determine the mass of the star fairly accurately. The first measurement is the timing: how long does it take for the planet to make one complete orbit. The second measurement is the orbital speed: how fast the planet is moving (or, equivalently and easier to measure, the star will wobble slightly because of the planet's gravity, so how fast is it wobbling?). This can be measured straightforwardly through Doppler shift measurements on the light coming from the star. So with these two measurements, we can use the equations that describe the orbit, and turn them around. We know the timing and the speed, so we can determine the size of the orbit and how heavy the central star must be. As long as our measurements are accurate (and they can be done very accurately these days), our estimate of the star's mass can be quite accurate as well, within a few percent in many cases. Edit: A lot of people like the say that we can't really know, or that it's'just theory'. But all it is, in many cases, is simple applications of basic laws of physics that we have tested very very thoroughly on Earth. The laws of orbital mechanics are very well understood; we use them every time we launch a satellite.,If you know what its made out of and how much of what its made out of weighs AND you know how big it is then you know the weight!

article: An average European worker tends to produce more value in a given hour of work than the average worker in an Asian country. A seamstress in Bangladesh will produce less value than a line operator at a Volkswagen plant. Europeans have far more capital (embodied both in physical stuff like the plant in my example as well as non-physical things like education) that allow them to be more productive, on average.','In a modern service economy most jobs don't generate a lot of wealth. Wealth generating activities, such as manufacturing, research, agriculture and mining, only employ a minority of workers. The bulk of workers is employed in wealth redistributing activities, such as sales, marketing, finance, administration, tax, regulatory affairs, etc. Those activities are zero-sum. Think of the economy as a collection of row boats. Pairs of "workers" sitting in each row boat are rowing in opposite directions and the boats stay more or less stationary. Each worker is fighting for his employer's share of wealth. Those opposing sides might be two competitors but could also be a government bureaucrat vs. a corporate bureaucrat. Now, if one side rows harder the other side also has to row harder in order to win back their slice of the pie. But the end result is that both sides are rowing harder but the boat still hasn't shifted position. In Europe, the government is more interventionist than in Asia (there are stricter labor laws) and mandates that both sides should row a little less hard. Since both sides are forced to oblige, it doesn't make much of a difference to their individual incomes, neither to the aggregate wealth of the economy.', "Culture - Europeans believe that life is worth living and that having to work every waking hour is basically slavery. We're not going to put up with it and neither should you.

article: When new fooddrink products are created, they're released in a test market. Basically, they release the product in a single city and see how it sells. If it sells well, they're release it in several cities in the area, then the state, then the neighboring states, then the country. That way, if it doesn't sell, they didn't product millions of bags of unsold candy that people hate. They might only produce hundreds of bags of unsold candy. If stuff's not in your area, it might be because a small town in central Ohio didn't like it. But a small town in central Japan did.," "There are a number of things in play when new goods are sold in a supermarket. In essence, it's down to economics, to launch a new product in any given market is a costly exercise. Not only does a manufacturer need to change or add new manufacturing capacity to make the product often and usually at great cost a manufacturer will also produce a multi-channel marketing campaign, this could be TV ads, Facebook, giveaways, and other promotional tools. If the manufacturer doesn't feel that there's a big enough market to be profitable once all those costs are taken into account it just doesn't make sense to launch. Another big factor is shelf space within the supermarket themselves. A lot of time and cost is involved in choosing and placing goods on shelves and with such limited physical space, it would require removing other and probably more profitable goods to be able to sell them. Even within a supermarket there's a big difference between place items at eye level, towards the ground or at the end of an aisle.," "Different products are coming from different branches of the company, a distributor bottler in Turkey is basically unconnected from one in the UK and do not have the same items. In many cases it comes down to preferences among the customers in that area, some places have people who like different flavours, are used to buying different flavours, or the market competition is different (maybe nobody else sells a Grape flavoured pop in Turkey) These companies do market research to see what their consumers want to buy, what works and what doesn't. People in Japan love kit-kats and buy a staggeringly huge amount of them because they symbolize good luck in Japan; also Japanese customers buy lots of different flavours. Financial is a big part, they do market research to know how much of what kind of product they sell, what their competition sells, and what people say they want to try.," " Is there a financial or logistical reason The financial reaosn is the company doesn't think they'd make money on those flavors in the UK, or already has another beverage in that category and don't want to compete with themselves.

article: So, let's boil it down to very, very basic terms. Your engine functions by pistons moving up and down. These pistons are attached to gears that turn their up-and-down motion into round-and-round motion, [which you can see here] (URL0). Now, in that GIF, see the silver parts? Those are the pistons, the part of your engine that is involved in the gasdiesel thing. These are moving inside of cylinders, which are just the parts of the engine that the piston moves up and down in. So the question is, what makes that piston go up and down? Here's where it gets kinda cool. Your car is driven by hundreds of tiny explosions. That's what gasoline and diesel are there for - to explode. What happens is this: your pistons come up to the top of the cylinder, and then the fuel injector sprays some fuel into the cylinder. The fuel is ignited (more in that in a moment) and that explosion drives the piston down, creating the motion that you see in the GIF. Now, what's different is how these things are ignited. One thing you have to know is that, when you compress something a lot, it heats up. So, in a diesel engine, as the piston comes up, it heats the air by compressing all the air in that cylinder into a tiny part of the cylinder. When your fuel injector sprays air in, it's so hot and pressurized, it ignites on its own and pushes the piston down. In a petrolgas car, fuel injection and ignition are done a bit differently. First, your fuel is mixed with air outside the cylinder, and that mixture is pumped in, and then ignited (diesels just toss some fuel into the cylinder's air rather than pre-mixing). The compression isn't enough to ignite the fuel, so you use spark plugs to basically create an electrical current that ignites the fuel - like dropping a live wire into a cloud of gas. So those are the main differences. Diesel: Mixed in your cylinder, ignited by compression GasPetrol: Mixed before it gets to your cylinder, ignited by sparks As for why it's used in one setting over another, diesel used to be a lot, lot dirtier than gas. It's a heavier, oilier substance, and put out a lot of soot and smoke. So car manufacturers used the cleaner-burning gasoline rather than diesel, for cosmetic and environmental reasons (nobody likes trailing a cloud of smoke, or being covered in soot at the end of a long commute). Recent advances made diesel a lot cleaner-burning, though, which has allowed us to make use of the big advantage that diesel has: energy density and efficiency. Energy density is how much energy a given amount of a substance has. When you burn a gallon of diesel, it puts out more energy than a gallon gasoline - about 18 more energy overall. Diesel engines are also more efficient than gasoline engines. Efficiency is how good your engine is at capturing that explosive energy from the piston and turning it into motion in your car. For various reasons, diesel engines (being slightly simpler in some ways) are much better at capturing more of that energy. So not only are they putting out more energy, but the diesel engine is capturing more of that bigger amount of energy than a gasoline motor could. That's why anywhere power and fuel efficiency are a concern (trucks, tractors, generators), diesel is preferred. You just get more bang for your buck, and then you capture more of that bang and turn it into motion. That's also why diesel-engine cars get really, really good miles-per-gallon they're taking advantage of that efficiency and energy density. FINALLY, why does diesel kill a gasoline-engine car? Well, remember that energy density? Your car is designed to withstand a very specific range of pressures. Diesel is so much more powerful, it can literally just break your engine's parts when it is ignited. The car has no way of knowing that and adjusting the mixture down to avoid it. So what happens? You pump in a lot more power into this engine, and BOOM - it just tears it apart with all that extra power that your gasoline-engine car isn't designed to handle.

article: In physics, there are lots of things that move in circles or rotate, so it's obviously useful there. It's way more interesting than that, though. Suppose you're on a Ferris wheel. I know how fast the Ferris wheel rotates, and what I'm interested in is knowing what height above the ground you're at at any given point in time. So, since Ferris wheels are circles, we'll study circles. Take a look at [this] (URL1). If you imagine that the circle is the Ferris wheel, y is your height at any given point in time (assume you're at point P). Because I took trigonometry in high school, I know that a mathematical function called the "sine function" is what gives me y. Specifically, sin (th) y, where th is the angle (you can see it labeled in the diagram). So, I know that sin (th) is what tells me how high you are at any given point in time. If I were to plot that on a graph, it would look like [this] (URL2). Like you'd expect, you're going up and down over and over as the Ferris wheel spins, it makes a lot of sense. Before I get too far ahead of myself, I want to remind you where sine comes from. It comes from a circle, it directly involves pi. There is no sine without pi, whenever I use sine, pi pops up. Alright, so when you look at the picture of the sine function, it looks sort of like a wave. It's actually typically called a "sine wave." That is not a coincidence. If we want to describe a wave in physics, we use sine (and cosine, its buddy). Sound waves? Sine. Light? Sine. Electrons? Sine. Literally any wave phenomenon, and I mean any wave phenomenon (other than water waves which are tricky) can be described in terms of sine. Not only that, but they can be described entirely using sine, you don't have to use anything else, ever. It's not just waves, either. Any sort of "oscillatory phenomenon," ie one that repeats itself over and over, we use sine. Pendulum? Sine. AC electricity? Sine. Vibrating string? Sine. Jiggling a slinky? Sine. Pi will rear its head whenever you try to talk about any of those things, as well as a bajillion other scenarios. At its heart, whenever we talk about "something that oscillates," it's the same as talking about your height as you ride a Ferris wheel. edit: [Here] (URL0) is an animation of how travelling around the "Ferris wheel" generates the sine function which I'm totally stealing from a post uDelehal just made.

article: Although killing bacteria is definitely a big deal, the most important thing about cooking is that it breaks down complex proteins, called denaturing. Proteins are very complex, and breaking them down into usable chunks takes energy. There are also complex sugars, like cellulose, that are just too big for us to digest without breaking them down a little first. That's why herbivores usually spend almost their entire day foraging, and why carnivores spend most of the day doing nothing. Energy is precious, animals can't afford to waste it. Herbivores need to eat constantly to get the energy they need and carnivores have to save what they have to spend it catching more food later. Humans, on the other hand, get way more usable energy out of food. Modern farming aside, we barely spend any time eating, and we get a huge boost of energy very soon after we eat. What do we do with all that extra energy? We get smarter. Human brains use a ridiculous 20 of our energy to fuel our brains. No animal comes close to that. And that massive energy expenditure is only possible because we cook our food first. It was certainly discovered by accident, probably animals caught in fires, or pre-humans using fire for light and heat accidentally dropped food in. It likely smelled pretty good. Over time and evolution, humans who favored the smell of cooked meat got more calories and reproduced. Mind, that's speculation, because we don't know for sure. That's also the opposite of the usual story, which is that pre-humans got smart and learned how to cook, rather than discovering cooking to get smart. [Here is an excellent TED talk on the subject] (URL0) All of that said, killing parasites and bacteria is also a really big deal. That should not be underestimated as something that has contributed to the evolutionary success of humans.

article: Keys work on a pinheight combination. When you look at your key, you'll see an even segment with tabs or flats. there's usually a large angled gap at the front and a notch at the back... these are sometimes correlated to pins that, if raised at all, block the lock (to make them a little bit harder to pick). So if you have 5 notchflat combinations on the elevated part of your key, the company just decides how many height tabs to use. It's merely a matter of manufacturing. A company could make an extremely delicate key with a thousand height settings, giving you a lot of possible combinations. Most companies use like 10 settings, giving them less combinations, but distribute them regionally in the hopes that there's little overlap. If you collect every key you ever possess, and try every key in every lock, you'll probably find one that works in a couple of different places. But consider the effort.," " How are all keys formed differently, with no overlap? They aren't. There are tons of identical keys out there. But the chance of one person attempting to use their key to unlock another lock that just so happens to use the same key is astronomically small. Remember, locks aren't there to keep out a dedicate thief. Someone intent on breaking into a building will just bust out a window, or break down the door. Locks are there to keep honest people honest by removing any temptation to enter somewhere where they're not allowed.," "There are certainly duplicates.
