article: Inside of your eye are specialized cells called [cone cells] (URL1) which give you your color vision. You have three types of cone cells: "S" cells pick up short wavelengths of light (blues violets), "M" cells pick up medium wavelengths (greens), and "L" cells pick up long wavelengths (reds). Between the three, you can see all the colors of the rainbow - ROYGBIV. Dogs, and in fact [almost all mammals] (URL0), have only two cone cell types: they don't have L cells like you do, so they're good at picking up on blues and greens (and related colors), but can't distinguish reds from those colors. On the other hand, many animals have [four types of cone cells] (URL2), the extra one often attuned to ultraviolet light. Fun fact: some humans have a mutant fourth cone - it doesn't seem to give them ultraviolet-vision, but it does give them better color perception than normal humans.', "I'm guessing all your doubts have been cleared by now, but if you're still interested in the subject, there's this science Podcast called Radiolab that has an episode dedicated to this. It's called [Colors] (URL3), and while it's a bit long, it is immensely entertaining and educational, not to mention insanely well produced. It made me fall head over heels with the show... I highly recommend it!

article: While linguists can reconstruct ancestor languages, those are just educated guesses as to what people used to say. article: even if it was obvious that they did it? Being "obvious" isn't enough. The prosecution has to prove that they did it, beyond a reasonable doubt. Something as wishy-washy as "it's obvious" would be a terrible basis for a legal system.', "A good defense lawyer's job is to plant a seed of doubt in the jury's mind. It could be obvious that he did it but if the lawyer can show how it was even remotely possible that someone else did it then the jury has to give him the benefit of the doubt. If he's good he'll take the remotest fact and stretch it into a reasonable doubt. They also work to get evidence thrown out. That was a lot of what happened with OJ, a lot of the best evidence that we saw on tv was never shown to the jury. I saw a special where they interviewed some members of the OJ jury a few years after the trial and they were pissed about the evidence they didn't get to see. They all said if they had seen some of those things the verdict might have been different. A good lawyer can find technicalities that can rule even some of the most damning evidence thrown out. The jury is only allowed to base their decision on what they see in the court room. The prosecutor must convince the jury that the guy did it and it is impossible that any one else could have. Any little bit of doubt, no matter how small, and the jury is not supposed to convict someone.,There must be admissible evidence which is sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The courts don't allow just any sort of innuendo or speculation to be presented to jurors. It may be "obvious" to people watching television that someone is guilty, but juries don't get the same information. And there is good reason for that, because the information reported by the media doesn't get the same scrutiny as the information presented to the jury. We want juries who decide people's fate to make their decisions for the right reasons and to base their reasoning on credible testimony and relevant evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. What is obvious to the public may seem "likely" to a person on the jury. But "likely" is not beyond a reasonable doubt. "Probably guilty" is not good enough for a conviction.

article: Now, in the interest of full disclosure, I am against gun control, I like guns, they're fun, they're great at what they do, and I think the world is a better place with the bang bang rooty tooty shooties in it. However, I'll try to be as unbiased as possible when laying out the arguments, I just wanted you to know my stance going into it to more easily spot any bias I have;) Let's get to it then I'm going to format this by the argument made and which side makes it followed by common rebuttal and the reply to that rebuttal from the side that posited the argument. Pro Gun Constitutional Right to "bear arms": Our 2nd Amendment Lays out this right which actually hearkens back to England during the 1500s I believe when every able-bodied man was considered to be part of the town's militia and was to bear arms in the case of an invader or to hunt down wolves killing people's sheep or protect the town from murderers etc. This is one of the most fundamental arguments because it's undeniable as being in the Constitution. This does, however, break down into arguments over what "bear arms" means and more commonly cited, the primary phrase of the Amendment which states "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State,..." which many people interpret to mean that the arms are to be borne by the militia (i.e. the national guard or other military branch). The interpretation of this very short Amendment has no real answer but the way that I interpret it (and many pro gun individuals do as well) is this: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed" breaks down to simple English as "Because we have to have a governmental body that needs a military to defend it and its people, in order to prevent tyranny, the people must have access to arms to defend themselves from the government if it so decides to turn on them." The Constitutional argument is honestly quite weak as far as actual rhetoric goes, however, because it's a document that can be changed, hell the Amendment itself is a change to the original document. Pro Gun It's My FreedomRight Similar to the Constitutional argument it's very fundamental and is often used to respond to the question "but why do you need a gun?." It's basically the argument that we should be able to do what we want because we are free people. Pro Gun Protection Argument This is one of the most used arguments that actually can have statistics used and empirical data employed. The argument here is that the purpose of a firearm is (among other things like hunting and sport) to be able to protect oneself and one's familyloved onesfriendswhatever needs protecting. The US Constitution has a set of amendments (the first ten, ratified way back in 1791) called the Bill of Rights. These have come to define a central part of the American concept of civil rights. One of these amendments is the 2nd Amendment, which sets aside a specific right to bear arms that "shall not be abridged." This amendment was originally demanded by anti-federalists in order to fulfill two roles; to make sure the citizenry would be appropriately armed to serve in militias, and to make sure that these militias would be well armed enough to challenge the federal government should it become necessary. At the time, this was a rather practical measure, since not only was gun ownership very common, but it was also a requirement for many people. Moreover, at the time republics of the sort they were experimenting with had essentially never really existed before and the anti-federalists didn't trust that the federal government being established by the Constitution would stay within its legal boundaries. So they demanded the 2nd amendment as a measure to assure that the government would not disarm the populace, and enable them to resist the government if required (which was a lot more feasible back then, since the US federal government was a weak and uncertain thing in 1791). Anyway, the social context of the United States has changed greatly in the intervening 200 years. We're now an advanced industrial state with a huge standing military, no need for militias, and a largely urban population contending with new issues like mass gun violence and suicide rather than threats that our now well established federal government is going to turn into some apocalyptic tyranny. But yet the 2nd amendment remains, and it prevents the federal government from taking any effective legal measures to reduce gun violence in the United States. The arguments that result are mainly about one group of people (the pro-gun-control group) who want to update statutory law to be more reflective of prevailing American society and concerns by imposing some level of gun control, and another group of anti-gun-control proponents who want to preserve a strict individual right to bear arms according to the 2nd amendment. This is the source of the tension, and currently this has been brought to a head by a rash of mass shootings that have captured popular attention, inflaming both sides. The pro-control side sees this as an example of everything they've been fighting to prevent for decades, and the anti-gun side now fears more than ever that the government is going to go grabbing guns, so they're arming up in record numbers.','The 2nd Amendment of the constitution reads: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed." (naw jokes GO HUMANITY WE NUMBAH 1) ', "Exoplanets, planets around stars other than the sun, have a couple of reasons they're important discoveries. For one, they tell us more about the composition and formation of the universe. Before we found any exoplanets, the only planets we knew about were those in our own solar system, and 8-9 planets is not a very big sample size. The big reason to study them is that the number of planets and their habitability are important parts of the [Drake Equation] (URL0), the formula for calculating how many other alien civilizations are out there and developed enough to be communicated with. Basically, if we know enough about the universe, we can figure out how likelyunlikely alien civilizations are with math. But to do that we need to know a lot of variables, like how many stars there are, how many stars have planets, how many of those planets are habitable, how many habitable planets develop life, how much life develops sentience, how many sentient species develop advanced communications technology, etc. Almost all of that stuff is difficult to figure out just from looking at earth. We need to look around at other stars to figure out how common planets are and how often they're in the habitable zone. Similarly, it's one of the main reasons scientists are interested in the possibility of microbial life on Mars. They know they're not going to find any advanced aliens that we could talk to, but even if they just find something like bacteria in Mars' extreme environment, that would indicate that planets are very likely to develop life and fill in a chunk of the equation.

EDIT: To clarify bad phrasing, the 4th amendment does actually declare some specific things to be private. Persons, houses, papers, and effects. He's just a lot better known.,Bruce Lee's legacy is difficult to qualify or explain, since his accomplishments were kind of unique. He was never a competitive fighter (aside from a high school boxing match that he won without even training for it). He was a gang member in Hong Kong as a teenager, so he did fight in the streets, which does establish that he had fighting experience in some form. But that tends to be the nagging question mark about Lee: how good of a fighter was he? Setting that aside for the moment, his accomplishments as an innovator in the martial arts are worth noting. He formulated Jeet Kune Do not as another style of martial art, but as a philosophy for how to create an ideal personalized martial art for oneself. He read J. Krishnamurti, Daisetz Suzuki, Alan Watts, et al., which gave him the idea that 'styles' of martial art and 'schools of thought' had a way of stifling our true natures and forcing us into a mold where we don't really fit. He was a talented athlete and a tireless trainer. Other notable martial artists of the day Chuck Norris, Mike Stone, Bob Wall, Jhoon Rhee, etc. have said that Lee trained harder than anyone they've ever seen. He would get an idea in his head and work on it for hours until he got it right. One time, for example, he wanted to see if he could drop a board from shoulder height and side kick it in half by the time it reached the level of his hip. He initially failed, and kept working on it for something like 7 hours that day until he could do it. If you try it, you'll see for yourself that it's very hard to do this. He always wrestled with the problem of how to develop power and speed in his offense. But I always question words like "great" when summing up someone's legacy. Lee was unique and innovative, and he also had camera presence and a flair for the dramatic. His family background in theater and the fact that he acted in films since he was 6 years old more or less foreordained that he would have a career in film. That was to be his way of becoming famous and making a living. In some ways, it's unfortunate that this is the only thing people know or remember about him i.e. his fame in the movies. People miss the complexity of the man when they only see his fame and the inevitable exaggerations that arise from it. People like to talk about his speed, which was amazing, and his one inch punch and lunging side kick. But he did those really as parlor tricks to demonstrate principles of martial art or superlatives of attribute development. Lee was fanatical about training his attributes. He wanted to overcome the stigma and stereotype of the Chinese as small and weak. He wanted to be their hero, and in fact he was. When people sitting in theaters saw that scene from "The Chinese Connection" where he's denied entry into a public park in Shanghai and he beats up all of the racist people taunting him, they really saw it as a statement about all Chinese people. He was their superman. He also taught himself film making camera work, directing, screenwriting, fight choreography, etc. So I suppose if we are to take anything from the sum of his accomplishments, the one truly "great" thing about him was his ability to self teach. He was a very dynamic thinker, and could basically figure out anything he put his mind to. There's a story about him as a teenager that illustrates the point. Lee trained in Wing Chun under Yip Man, but he also wanted to learn other styles of Gung Fu so that he could figure out their weaknesses and defeat them if he ever had to fight them in the streets of Hong Kong. Meanwhile in that time the Choy Li Fut master had only begun to learn the basics of Cha Cha. People who are wowed by Lee as a Kung Fu movie star tend to overlook the things about Lee that were really "great," in my opinion. He was a voracious reader, and he studied everything that interested him. He had this unshakeable belief in his own ability to learn or do anything. He had a lucid way of analyzing things that he studied and penetrating the complexity of something to get to its essence. This inspired people around him, since one rarely encounters someone who is so dynamic as a human being. article: The sugar, even in powdered form, retains a certain crystal structure. When in contact with water (in your mouth) it requires a certain amount of energy to "break" this structure and dissolve. article: Someone creates a story, called a DM. Other someones create characters. The story can either be very planned out, or something that gets made up on the spot or a mix. Sometimes, you can buy a full "story" in a box, and then the DM just runs the story and adds color as the characters play. the game itself is all the rules that allow you to decide what happens in the story, and what the characters are like. This can be everything from a way to decide whether an arrow hits it's target, or how many spells a wizard has, or what the odds are of getting randomly targeted by thieves when traveling between cities. But the DM and the players are free to tweak these if they think it will be more fun.','Dungeons and dragons is a tabletop roleplaying game. Essentially, players take the role of characters and interact in a shared, imagined world. One player acts as the "dungeon master" who facilitates the game by being the one in charge of creating and managing the world, non-player characters, and other things the player characters interact with. This is pretty much how all tabletop role playing games work. The rules described in D D's books lay out a framework for how to resolve actions in the game world. Generally the way actions are resolved in D D is by rolling a 20 sided die (with a bonus applied to indicate how good your character is at performing the action) and attempting to surpass some specific number that indicates the action was successful. If I want my character to swim across some raging river rapids, the dungeon master assigns a difficulty to the action (say, "20," meaning my roll on the 20 sided die plus my character's bonus for swimming must meet or exceed 20 in order for my character to successfully swim across). That's the basics of how the game works, anyway.', "Imagine a collaborative session of writing an episode of a fantasy action-adventure series. The producerdirector comes to the table with the bones of a story - the main guest stars, the basic plot, the goals and challenges and aims that will make up the framework. However, instead of sharing the whole thing with the team, he only shares the introduction to start with - and everyone else gets into character and takes the initiative to drive it along from inside the story. As they go along, the DM keeps the reins, introduces scenarios and characters relevant to the plot, vetoes anything too silly OP out of character, to keep the story more or less on course. There can be formal rules and stats (equivalent to a'show bible to determine what characters can and can't get away with. A wizard might be mighty, but he can't just fireball his way through an entire army (rinse and repeat for warrioirs, archers, priests, etc); there are tables of figures determining the exact powers and limits thereon that people and monsters have. To prevent conclusions from being foregone, outcomes are often determined by dice rolls - performing a feat of strength successfully would require you to roll a number lower than your'strength' stat, for instance. The DM also enforces limits on what characters would do say put up with, for instance. If you're in a party of goody-two-shoes types and you decide to torture your enemies for information, the others won't be allowed to stand for it. 'Winning', or having the characters reach their stated objective, is not a mandatory goal of the DM. They're meant to be given the opportunity, but it shouldn't be guaranteed by any means.," "In simple terms, it's a story telling game for 2 or more people. One person controls everything about the world to make a story. Everyone else is a main character in that story. There are rules so that you can't make believe everything you want, that would get out of hand. There are several books filled with mythological creatures, beings, treasures, and magic to use for your world. But the books are only a guide for your imagination, it's not limited by them.

article: In theory, anything that isn't encrypted. If you're using a website with HTTPS you should be fine, although a bad guy might still be able to see the fact that you're connecting to that website. If you need more security than that, consider a VPN.,The answer is "It depends on your ISP" When DOCSIS (the protocol on which the cable modem talks back to your ISP) was first introduced, there was no encryption on the data between your modem, and the ISP. DOCSIS being a radio frequency protocol (just constrained inside the wire) is based on broadcasts, and the modems were set to just ignore everything that was not addressed to you. This meant that anyone on your node, which is usually most or all of your entire neighborhood, could hook a modified device up to the cable plant and listen to everything that everybody else in the neighborhood did that was not through HTTPS. DOCSIS version 1.1 introduced something called BPI, or Baseline Privacy Interface, the is what is important here. The original DOCSIS had something called BPI which is part of what told each modem the 'address' to listen for, and BPI added encryption to each individual modem using a key exchange much in the same way that HTTPS uses SSL (This was originally 56bit DES, and has since been improved to 128bit AES in BPI SEC which was introduced with DOCSIS 3.0) Now here is the tricky part, and why the answer still is "It Depends on your ISP." All of the encryption features are completely optional, and are not enabled by default. They are quite simple to implement (on the ISP side) and I don't personally know of any ISPs that are not running at least the 56bit DES version of BPI on their plants (as it also helps prevent theft of service), I am sure there are a few out there that have not enabled it.

This presumption is not absolute. Traps are normally defending unoccupied property, where self-defense doesn't work. However, even for occupied property, some jurisdictions consider them unjustifiable force. The traditional rule was that traps were justified only if a person in the same situation would have been justified in using deadly force (if you ignore that adding a person to unoccupied property makes it occupied). So, to discourage people from trying to game the odds, the rules have been generally changed to make deadly traps unreasonable. article: why couldn't we just get a cramp, run to the bathroom and be done in 10-20 minutes like a bowel movement from the front bottom? An even better question is why you need to do it at all! Only primates, bats, and the elephant shrew even have overt menstruation (bleeding from the vagina), the rest of the mammals manage without it. At the end of their reproductive cycle they simply reabsorb their endometrium internally, no fuss no muss. Many zoologists view this as the "true" menstrual cycle and the primate's bloody version a weird departure. Instead it seems that human embryos are somewhat more prone to genetic abnormalities so the mother has developed a greater hormonal control over the implantation of an embryo rather than in other species where the embryo takes a greater role in implantation. Being able to shed the uterine lining then may be a defense against abnormal embryos, saving valuable resources which would otherwise be spent on nonviable offspring and returning the womb to business in a shorter period of time. URL0','The uterus' main function is to house and grow an egg into a baby, and then to host said baby for 9 months and gently expell it. This is vastly different from the main function of the colon, which is built of muscles used for squeezing and crushing and quickly and efficiently expelling feces. When you have your period, your body is essentially "killing" the tissue built for a (now unfertilized) egg, and has to expell all of that. Using muscles that are not made with the main function of expelling in mind. If it were made of the same muscles (and muscle functions) as the colon, a baby would be forcibly pushed out in a poo shape within a few hours of conception, like is done with poo. But pooping isn't the main function of your uterus, and neither is the period. Thus, it hurts and it leaks and it sucks. Such is life. Edit: typo.

article: Anything that isn't at absolute zero emits thermal radiation. The atoms and molecules are jiggling around (that's what temperature means), and when they bump into each other and stuff, photons get emitted. We call those photons "thermal radiation." The hotter the substance is, the higher energy photons it will emit. So, for example, a lightbulb works by running electricity through a filament. The filament gets really hot, so it emits lots of thermal radiation. It's hot enough that the photons have enough energy to be in the visible light spectrum, which is why it makes visible light. Most objects at regular Earth temperatures are much cooler than a lightbulb. At those temperatures, the bulk of the thermal radiation emitted is infrared. You can think about it this way: when you get something really hot, it starts glowing red. Before it reaches that temperature, though, it's emitting radiation with less energy than red light, ie infrared.', "Any wavelength in the Electromagnetic spectrum can transfer heat. If you radiate more heat, you get higher frequencies of electromagnetic radiation. IR radiation is just what's common to the temperatures around what we're used to.

article: Red, green, and blue (RGB) are the primary colors for light (i.e., additive color). In this case, "black" is the absence of any light, and "white" is 100 of all three colors. Cyan, yellow, and magenta (CYM) are the primary colors for pigment (i.e., substractive color). In this case, "white" is the absence of any pigment, and "black" is 100 of all three pigment colors. Each of these pigments get their color from absorbing one of the primary light colors, and reflecting the other two. Thus cyan is the mix of green and blue (absorbs red), yellow is the mix of red and green (absorbs blue), and magenta is the mix of red and blue (absorbs green). The "K" in CYMK is "black." Printers will often add a separate reservoir of black ink for darker shades of color and for black white printing. EDIT: Bolded some terms and added language for clarity.

article: All the major news outlets are businesses attempting to maximize their profits. All news outlets consider themselves "biased towards the center" but they need to differentiate themselves from their competitors if they want to survive. As the audience changes, the major news outlets need to shift their biases to keep up. Otherwise some other news outlet will steal their audience. Media bias is just a weird topic to me, I don't see why there can't be news outlets that provide real, undramatized news that respect both the right and left so that people can form their opinions for themselves. This is impossible due to the problem of "anchoring." Consider a world where people on the right want the tax rate to be 1 lower and people on the left want the tax rate to be 1 higher. The news outlet reports both sides with equal respect. Then one side decides to play a little trick, and declare that they want the tax rate to change by 90 instead of 1. Now what is the news outlet supposed to do? If they treat this proposal with respect, they are biased towards the radicals. If they don't treat this proposal with respect, they are biased towards the other side. The news outlet has to make a decision on what is and is not reasonable, and that decision will always be considered biased by somebody.', "Actually, the early days of mass journalism (120 years ago or so) were even more biased than today's media. As newspapers consolidated, they found they could attract a bigger audience and make more money by shifting to the center. They also started facing competition from TV and radio, so they cultivated prestige and high journalistic standards as a way to compete. As others have pointed out, it's nearly impossible to completely eliminate bias, so papers like the NYT or the WSJ do have a distinct editorial slant. But they also feature solid researchsourcing, and do their best to keep their reporting and editorial content as separate as possible. Early TV news was somewhat similar. There were high capital and regulatory barriers to become a TV network, so until the late 80s, there were basically only 3. Since they had the same need to attract a large audience across the political spectrum, and had a certain degree of government oversight (under the theory that the frequency bands that they used were a public good, so they had to play by certain rules to have access to them), they copied the newspapers with in-depth reporting, careful attention to sources and accurate facts and so on. The big game-changer was cable (and then the internet). Since cable used private infrastructure instead of public airwaves, they didn't have to play by the same rules, and because the number of channels grew, moving away from the center became a way to differentiate yourself from the other news outlets. Competing for a larger slice of a smaller pie, as it were. Also, with so many channels, sensationalizing your content became a plus that would attract viewers instead of undermining your credibility. Also, with the rise of 247 cable news channels starting with CNN, stations had more time than they could possibly fill merely reporting the news. So editorial content (which by it's nature is guaranteed to be more biased than straight reporting) took over.," "It is impossible to write something without any accusations of bias. Imagine the editor of the local crime desk at a newspaper when a murder occurs. If you include the race of the perpetrator you will receive accusations of bias from one side, and if you omit it you will receive them from others. And that's just one choice of dozens that you'd have to make over the simplest article. Further, the news model changed dramatically when people stopped paying for it. In the past, newspapers supported themselves with classified ad revenue and subscriptions, so they could afford to weather the loss of advertisers and limit their influence on the editorial staff. Now, since every one consumes news for free, the advertisers have much more sway over content.," "Try an exercise for yourself and make a small one paragraph report on some argument two of your friends had or your parents had. Then, present it to those people and ask them to critique it. They will find some sort of bias in it because human beings cannot write completely objectively. I mean, say you report that your friend was yelling at your other friend. How do you define yelling and determine if somebody was yelling or they weren't yelling? Whatever criteria you use, somebody can cast doubt on it and consider your writing biased and say they were not yelling because it doesn't fit their criteria for yelling.,Manufacturing Consent by Noam Chomsky taught me a lot about media bias and how the elite sections of the society (political and business leaders, etc.) use the media to present a favorable image of themselves before the public.

article: What's actually inverted is back to front, without changing leftright or updown. If it instead flipped leftright (and only left-right) while you're facing it, you'd be seeing the back of your head, but with your right ear on the left hand side, and so on. If you want to see a mirror with both back to front and leftright flips, you can set that up. Have a look at URL0 for a diagram: You basically make a 90deg angle corner out of two mirrors, then look into the corner. Making a mirror that doesn't flip backfront is much harder; easiest way is to put two mirrors on opposite walls, stand between them, then try to look around yourself in the mirror. That won't flip left-right either. However, that setup is cheating a bit, though. I'm sure you could do some sort of periscope-like setup if you wanted it properly done, and one could probably even get it to flip left-right alone, but, frankly, it's probably easier just to put a some sort of webcam behind your head, facing you, and look at what it's broadcasting, and tell the software to flip it leftright or not as you prefer. By the way, a back-front flip and a rotation aren't the same thing. If you have a camera and aim it at you, then look at what it's broadcasting, you'll find it's similar to looking at a non-reversing mirror. It's actually rather strange and offputting. Programs like Skype will flip the image for you (but not the person you're talking to) in order to compensate for the differences; this works really well.... until you hold up a book to the camera or wear a shirt with text on it. To understand the difference between a flip and a rotation, try this: Open two copies of MSPaint, and paste an image into it. Go to Image- FlipRotate. With one, choose Flip vertical, with the other, choose rotate 180deg. Compare. article: The main difference between the effects of an atomic bomb detonated in space and that on the ground are not related to gravity, but are related to the fact that the bomb is going off without an atmosphere (air) around it. When a bomb goes off, a lot of the energy is released as thermal and ionizing radiation (heat radiation and nuclear radiation). In an atmosphere (that is, relatively near the surface of the Earth or on it), a good amount of that energy is immediately absorbed into a shell of air surrounding the bomb. This super hot shell of air then bursts out, causing the well-known pressure (blast) effects of the bomb - the stuff that knocks down houses and smashes everything. In the absence of an atmosphere, the heat and nuclear radiation are not as dissipated, and the blast pressure is much more muted. As a result, a nuclear weapon detonated in space is mostly heat and nuclear radiation, and both of those effects go further than they would on Earth, because they are not being absorbed by any atmosphere. The other main difference is that the electromagnetic pulse effect of the bomb, which is relatively limited at near-surface altitudes, can go much, much further and be much more powerful. This can disable satellites and even certain types of electrical circuits on Earth, over a very wide area. As with all high airbursts, there would be no local nuclear fallout. The radiation, however, can linger in space for a long time, which has implications for satellites and radio communications. There would be no mushroom cloud, which is a function of the fireball being in an atmosphere as well. (The fireball is hot and less dense than the atmosphere, so it rises. The movement of a less dense substance through a dense one produces the familiar mushroom-cloud appearance.) Gravity has no effect on allowing the blast to expand or compressing it. It is too weak a force to affect that. It is not possible to make a black hole from a nuclear explosion; black holes are formed by putting lots of matter into one place. A nuclear explosion does not do anything like this.

Usually, the electrons are zipping around the protons and there is an equal balance of electrons (negative charge) and protons (positive charge). Basically, every electron has a "home base" which is an atom or molecule. A "regular" plasma is when you heat up matter enough that the electrons go zipping out of their home bases and you have a soup of electrons and protons and stuff all mixed together. This requires very high temperatures, like in a blowtorch or on the surface of the Sun. Turns out that if you have enough energy in one place, the protons (and neutrons) themselves will split up into even smaller bits called quarks. Gluons are particles that hold quarks together (like glue. Yes, for real.). This requires INSANE amounts of energy, but it's what we think the universe was like right after the Big Bang. All of these random quarks can reconfigure into weird types of matter, so scientists can study what comes out to see what was happening during the plasma phase. TL:DR Heat stuff up enough and it "melts" into crazy tiny particles called quarks.

article: You'll need to be more specific about which'flat map'. It's affected by your choice of map projection. But I believe for a standard Mercator projection no, flying due east (except at the equator) isn't a great circle and you're flying along a line of constant latitude.,A straight line on a globe appears as a curve on a flat map, since projecting the curved earth on a flat image creates distortion. I think that more or less answers your question.','If you used a compass to fly in any direction, it would be a straight line on a Mercator projection. Other projections, it depends (due east, west, north, or south would probably be straight lines on a lot of maps but again, it depends). In a Mercator projection, "rhumb lines" are straight lines. A rhumb line is the path you would take if you maintained a constant compass heading (important for naviation). As your latitude changes, a constant heading actually points in a slightly different direction because you are getting closer to the magnetic pole. Ever wonder why Mercator projections never show the North or South Pole? They can't - a rhumb line that isn't due north or south will theoretically spiral around the pole forever, so the poles are at positive and negative infinity... A Lambert projection has the pole at the center and the lines of latitude are circles around it. This projection has the characteristic that Great Circles are straight lines. You can't show the equator on a Lambert projection because it would be infinite distance from the pole (because the equator, being a great circle, would have to be a straight line....) ','The shortest distance between two points on a globe follows the path of a circle around the circumference of that globe, connecting those two points. While not answering your first question, this is why looking at a flight path appears arced on a map. So the flight path is not "due east." If you followed a compass due east, walking or flying, you would appear to make a straight line on a standard map, but at least by air you would not be taking the shortest route to your destination.

article: This is a Keurig.] (URL1) As you can see, it's a coffee maker you put a little cup into, which is about the same shape and size as a shot glass, and is filled with coffee grounds or other stuff. The machine ranges from 80 to 120 to occasionally more. The cups, however, range anywhere from 50 cents to over 1 each. Each cup contains 0.40 oz of coffee. If you drink three 1 cups a day and use the Keurig for all of them, you're spending about 90 a month on the cups. However, if you buy a big tub of Folgers (33.9 oz) and pack the same amount (0.40 oz) into a refillable keurig cup, you'll be spending about 8 a month on coffee instead. So obviously, the company makes an immense profit on the cups, but not so much on the machines. Refillable and off-brand cups cut directly into the Keurig company's sales, and since their [patent ran out] (URL0), there's no legal way for them to stop the off-brands. So they want to make the next machine they make (keurigs only last so long) to ONLY accept THEIR brands of cups. In their ideal world, you put in an off-brand cup and the machine doesn't work. This part is mostly speculation, because I couldn't find anything that says what exactly the DRM is. There are three ways I see that this could work. First and most likely, there's a barcode printed on the side of each cup, and the keurig reads it like a scanner. No barcode, or an incorrect barcode, and the machine doesn't work. Second way would be to make both the cups and the insert slot a really weird shape, making it much less likely an off-brand would fit both the keurig machine and their own brand. Finally and by far the least likely, each cup gets a microchip that the machine reads. Personally, I don't see this as turning out well for Keurig. The biggest reason by far that people use the keurig is convenience. If it becomes a hassle, people will stop using it.

article: The image created by night vision is blackwhite. Human eyes are most sensitive to green light. This is why the Bayer pattern used in many cameras has two green pixels, one red pixel, and one blue pixel per quad. article: Just to follow on from some of the earlier answers: LCD screens have multiple layers to them, so need to have somewhere to route the cables to the middle layer. You can't do this from behind without drilling a hole through the back layer - which is the backlight - and leaving a dead patch on the screen. Even if you put all these wires on one side, the remaining three sides still need something to hold all the layers together - putting glue between them would hurt the image quality. That said, there's no reason the frame couldn't be made from a transparent plastic, transparent aluminium, or another see through material. It would look ugly from an angle where you can see the layers, which is probably the only reason it hasn't been done. Edit to add: Also, light bleeding. You probably don't want light from the backlight illuminating the stand during a dark scene - as some would be leaking out the bottom and sides of the screen without going through the image layers, the surroundings would be illuminated bright white, which would produce glare on the picture that could drown out darker scenes.," "For protection againts shock, so the screen doesn't break easily. It will actually hard to operate a full-touchscreen cell phone without bezel (you have to change the way you hold the phone, so it doesn't touched accidentally),The wires that connect to the display to send the image have to go somewhere.', "From a design standpoint, the bezel sets the screen apart from the background, so they don't bleed together. She has the defective, dormant gene too. Do the math, and you get a 1 in 4 chance of having a baby with that weird disease or defect. One of your kids will probably get that defective gene from both parents, meaning it WILL be expressed, i.e. it will be in charge and you will have the defect associated with it. This article gives a good layman explanation of this issue in relation to dog breeding: genetica on webarchive (copy whole link, cant get it to work with reddit formatting?): URL2 Signs of inbreeding in animal populations are: small (er) litters, less robust immune systems and various hereditary diseases getting'fixed' in the breed. So anybody getting a pure breed pet - make sure that you ask about the inbreeding both over 6 generations and total numbers. A responsible breeder will know. I just found one randomly with total inbreeding of 40...,Think of it in terms of mixing colors of paint. If you mix red and blue, you get purple. On the other hand, people who sell virgin paper, or paper that's not easily recyclable, emphasize how white and smooth it is. As well as having fillers like clays, high quality paper is made with fresh, long cellulose. Each time it's pulped a fraction of the fibers will be broken. As the average length goes down, so does the properties of the paper. Factors like tear strength and flexibility vs thickness contribute to the quality, so recycled pulp tends to be used for things like cardboard, kitchen towel, toilet paper and suchlike.

article: I get why they would want you to call them or visit them, but wouldn't making the process easier be better for their business? Not necessarily. If I'm looking for martial arts classes for example, and I can price-check online, I'd be less likely to ever consider anyone but the cheapest. Once you're actually checking the place out, going in there, etc., you're more likely already to choose that place. They want you to come in to be convinced the price is reasonable, and not be openly outbid by their competition. Usually you see this in places where the "going rate" for the service isn't well-defined. If dude has a nice studio, took a lot of classes himself, and thinks his expertise is worth it, it's better for him to charge what he thinks is right and leave it to you to figure out if there's a better deal out there. article: Nodes can be logging, it doesn't matter. However, every node only knows about the predecessor and the upcoming node. Plus - unless it's the exit router - it's protected by a layer of symmetric keys of all upcoming nodes. So, you get a problem if the exit router is evil - he'll be the one who is last in decoding the message, thus seeing it clearly. Therefore you should always use end-to-end protection protocols like TLSSSL additionally.

article: Aquatic biologist here. I think the real question is "why are open ocean fish so dull"? A great many reef fish are colorful, so are a great many freshwater fish, especially those that aren't "open water" fish. Really, many fish are very colorful or boldly patterned. I think the answer is "because they can be." Open water fish (ocean or freshwater) live in a solid blue environment with nothing to hide behind. They are often (but not always) that classic silvery or flat blue fish color. But fish near reefs (or in small streams) have other options. They have shelter to hide behind if they spot a predator (meaning camouflage isn't as important). That means they can more easily use brilliant colors as social or sexual signals. If they want to be camoflaged, they can use color or pattern as a means to hide rather than being limited by a featureless environment.

article: Most animal models of cancer use mice without an immune system, and they just inject some cancer cells from a flask into the mouse. Different cancer cells sometimes spread to different parts of the body (e.g. Lung cancer cells spreading to the lungs) and some just form a tumour at the site of injection. Other animal models can use a chemical that causes cancer to induce tumours. Source- PhD student in a cancer research lab Edit- because the mice don't have an immune system, they don't try to get rid of the cancer, because those cells will be foreign to the mouse, the same as bacterial cells that our immune system can attack,Tumor cells are grown in a dish and injected into the rodent. Different types of tumors grow in different injection sites (and grow better in certain places or in specific strains of animals etc). For example, breast cancer cells can grow into a tumor in several places but tend to grow well in the mammary fat pad of female rodents. You can also model metastases by injecting your tumor cells intravenously- they will hit the lungs on their way around, and will settlegrow there.','One method is implanting tissue directly from a patient. Once a patient signs a consent form, a portion of the tumor is brought to the research lab. Immune-compromised micerats are knocked out using anesthetic, an incision is made, and a small piece of the tumor is implanted in the animal just under the skin. When it grows to a large enough size, the tumor is extracted, spilt into many pieces, and implanted in many more mice (or frozen for later use, or collected for analysis, etc.). This is repeated to maintain stocks of mice with the desired tumor type, some of which are then used for studies. Source: do this for a living.','Besides injection of cells, there are genetic models. For breast cancer, there are a couple different extremely well known lines of mice that are extremely predisposed to tumors. For liver cancer, there is a chemical you can inject into baby mice that predisposes them to tumors later in life.','I did some research on melanoma using mice this summer, I can help answer this! My specific project was actually perfecting the method of giving mice cancer to use them as models for cancer treatments. Basically, we order cancer cells from a company that has made a consistent, pure cell line. We feed the cells a nutrient-rich cell food and let them multiply on a plate, then inject the cells right into the mouse and let them do their cancer thing. For our purposes, we injected the mice in the ear since it has a nice supply of blood and the mice couldn't mess with the growing tumors too much (they tend to scratchgnaw at them because tumors smell weird to mice). You can also use a "seed" or "donor" mouse, where you do the same process as above, let the tumor get freakin' huge, euthanize the mouse, cut out the tumor, then mash it into a tumor smoothie and inject THAT into another mouse. This supposedly works better as the cells are adapted to living mice already, but don't quote me on that. Since our project was about measuring immune responses, our mice had fully functioning immune systems. This means that half the time the mice actually resisted the cancer, which was a bummer for our study but good for the mice I guess lol.','They breed rats that have genetic mutations. The other way is to expose them to chemicals and radiations that cause mutations at an early age.', "There are a variety of methods, and it all depends on the cancer and what you're researching which method is utilized. If you're trying to prevent cancer, or see how something interacts with cancerous progenitors, you might use a gene mutation that's known to promote cancerous tumor growth, or expose the group to a carcinogen, and then do a variety of things to see which treatment limits growth or occurrence the most. You can also implant tumors or cancerous cells, which others here have described. You can also do a variety of the above, like irradiate them, expose them to cigarette smoke, and then stress them, and compare rates of growth to a null group, etc.," "I'm a lab student and had to do a research with tisseu from lab rats with cancer. For this research they injected cancerous cells, from the kind of tumor they wanted to study, into a rat. article: Basically, SN1 favors stability, and SN2 favors a quick attack. If you have a large structure with many carbons attached to it, andor with many conjugated bonds (which also increase stability) See benzene, SN1 will likely be favored thermodynamically. There are still reactions with SN2 models on larger compounds, but they are less common and will probably not be tested over. SN2 would not be favored in the in large bulky compounds because of steric hindrance. SN2 does that back attack thing remember? It likes to shoot in really fast and not bump into anything on it's way. SN2 favors a strong nucleophile (negatively charged) which basically attacks the nucleus (positively charged) quickly. There are reactions that you can do at low temperatures that will favor SN1 because of it's love for stability and a thermodynamically favorable product, but will favor SN2 at high temperatures. Why? Well SN2 is fast and doesn't care about stability, and SN1 is slow and careful. Edit: To clarify this section, slowing down the reaction will favor the formation of thermodynamically stable products, while speeding up a reaction favors the product that forms most quickly. So in a most basic sense, if you see a very stable molecule andor a weak nucleophile, it will be SN1. If you see a unstable molecule as you carbo-cation andor a strong nucleophile (strong base in most cases) it will be SN2 because a quick reaction will take place. Solvent is also important, but I can't go into that because it's been too long. Something about polar proticaprotic or something. Good luck and I hope that helps clear things up.

article: Interpol doesn't actually investigate anything or have any jurisdiction. It just facilitates contact between police departments in different countries. For example, lets say you're a police officer in Chicago who is investigating a criminal that fled overseas, but you don't know where. Without Interpol it would be very difficult, if not impossible to find that person. With Interpol you can send them your warrant and they will then put the warrant into a database that other nation's law enforcement agencies check against. So your criminal tries to cross an international border somewhere. When they do that, the local customs agents will check them against Interpol's database, discover that they are wanted in Chicago, and then arrest them so they can be extradited. It also helps out in investigations between different countries. Again, lets say you're investigating a human trafficking ring that spans multiple countries. Without Interpol it would be difficult to impossible to know what other countries also had law enforcement working on the same case as you, and you would have similar troubles figuring out who to contact in those countries even if you did find out they were conducting a parallel investigation. With Interpol, you can send them a notice giving them a rough outline of what you're investigating and they will check that against what other law enforcement agencies are also telling them. If Interpol sees that both you and a law enforcement agency in another country are investigating the same thing, they'll put you in contact with one another. Likewise, if you want an investigation started in another country Interpol will know who to put you in contact with to get that started.," "Yeh Interpol itself doesn't have officers, or agents that they send around to do police work, it's essentially an organisation to allow different police forces around the world to work together. So say if a criminal from her in the UK fled to Canada, police officers would, via Interpol, be able to get Canadian officers to arrest the fugitive.

article: Simple probability, like what you'd use for a coin flip, doesn't care about previous outcomes. After 2 coin flips coming up heads the next one is still 50:50. You could try to logic your way into claiming that the next one will more likely be heads since you're on a streak of heads, or you could try to logic your way into claiming the next one will likely be tails because the streak has to end sometime. Both are equally wrong and are examples of the gambler's fallacy. A sequence of 10 heads in a row is uncommon simply because there are so many different 10-toss sequences (1024 of them; that's 2 (10. Each of those 1024 sequences is equally improbable. Note that there are some systems where past events do have predictive power. A classic example is the weather: if you're living somewhere where it rains 50 of days then you may be able to get a better than 50 chance at guessing the weather tomorrow if you consider whether it rained today or not. This is Bayesian Statistics. It isn't applicable to independent events like different tosses of a fair coin.,Odds of flipping 10 straight 10 heads. After 0 flips: 1 out of 1024 (0.098) After 1 Flip Heads: 1 out of 512 (0.195) After 2 Flips Heads: 1 out of 256 (0.391) After 3 Flips Heads: 1 out of 128 (0.781) After 4 Flips Heads: 1 out of 64 (1.563) After 5 Flips Heads: 1 out of 32 (3.125) After 6 Flips Heads: 1 out of 16 (6.250) After 7 Flips Heads: 1 out of 8 (12.500) After 8 Flips Heads: 1 out of 4 (25.000) After 9 Flips Heads: 1 out of 2 (50.000) ', "Probably would be easier to understand if you can visualise it. Take a piece of paper and draw a big V, one branch is heads, the other is tails. Then draw a smaller V from each branch, again 1 of each of these branches is heads and tails. Keep going until you have 10 levels. Now you have all the possible combinations of flipping a coin 10 times. You'll notice that only 1 of all of these paths through the 10 levels is all heads or all tails. There are hundreds of other combinations that aren't the one you want.,Because the chain of 10 in a row has a probability of (0.5) 10. To expand: That's a very low probability. Probably you're thinking why the tenth flip itself has a low probability, but it doesn't. In itself it has the same probability as a single toss, 0.5, or 50. But that has to follow the very slim probability of having already flipped 9 in a row, so "getting there" is the problem.', "Every combination of 10 flips has the same probability. 10 heads in a row just feels special because it's an easily identifiable pattern.

article: While electronics perform better, chemical reactions are typically slower at low temperatures. So at some point, the battery will not be able to deliver enough power to the phone, and it will shut down.', "In general, the colder the temperature, the better a material will conduct electricity. Cold not only reduces electrical resistance, it also prevent heat from building up. This is usually a good thing, but it could be bad if it causes a component to receive more current than it was designed for. Also, cell phones aren't just electronic devices. They are chemical devices, with batteries that do not produce as much current in the cold. They also have glass components, which might crack from the temperature differential between a hot CPU and cold air.," "Low temperatures can cause condensation to form inside the device, which is a big problem for complex electronics with circuits tightly packed together. That's why it's better not to operate them at low temperatures.

article: I studied brain science in university, so I'll take a crack at this. It's neither. It's a predictive statement that describes how likely the person is to do well at the sort of tasks one does in school. That's what it was designed for. Yes, it's possible for a person to raise their IQ score somewhat through training, perhaps as much as 10-15 points if it was not high to begin with.," "IQ is a very rough estimate of intelligence. Without nerding out over a bunch of statistical mumbo jumbo, it works much better as a statistic for groups than for individuals. For example, if experiments show that adding an hour per week of homework increase IQ by an average of 5 points that will likely carry over to other groups of students. On an individual level it's much less useful. 80 vs 130 is a big difference so you're likely to see differences in aptitude but you might not. If the kid with the 80 IQ is an ESL student their result could be downward biased. If the kid with the 130 IQ had parents who coached them on how to take IQ tests (as my parents did) that score is likely to be biased upward. As you also noticed, hard work makes a huge difference. If the kid with the 80 IQ is busy practicing writing while the kid with the 130 IQ is busy minmaxing his Pokemon collection there's a good chance that the kid with the higher IQ could end up looking like the slow one at the end of the year.," "The best analogy I've read is to engine displacement. For most driving tasks, a little 4-cylinder 2L engine will be as effective as a 6-cylinder 3L one. Sure, the 3L car will start going a little quicker, but it's a lot less fuel efficient. The students with higher IQ might pick something up more quickly but might also be more likely to be distracted when the class moves at a pace all the students can keep up with. The students with lower IQ might always be working their hardest, but when they stay focused they can keep up. In car engines, for most trips to the grocery store the difference isn't really relevant. That's mostly the same with learners.," "The thing about IQ is that it isn't linear. A person with an 80 isn't half as capable as a person with 160, for example. People as low as 50 can do simple labor jobs and take care of themselves alright. And as long as you're patient with teaching a person with a lower IQ, they can pick up just as much as a person with a high IQ. They might not make the same connections or be able to make the jump from the basics to the complicated parts, but they'll slowly pick it up.

article: People are dying less of infectious diseases in the developed world today. Causes of death here in North American tend to be heart disease and cancer. You can think of it as more people dying of cancer because everything else didn't have the chance to kill them first. Getting cancer is pretty much inevitable because it's not so much something that directly gave you cancer so much as your body failing to correct some damage caused (and it can be caused by almost anything including sunlight, contact with other humans, being near concrete, eating food, breathing oxygen, etc.) and that damage coincidentally leading to cells that keep dividing and refuse to die. You are actually getting things like cancer all the time, but your body is good at error detection and destroying compromised cells. This is also why a singular "cure for cancer" is sort of a silly concept right now. Cancer is an entire categorization of things, and it's completely possible to have a completely unique cancer. What can be worked on are treatments for cancer and cures for very specific cancers. Childhood leukemia, for example, has a cure rate of 90, and we are approaching the point where we can sort of call it cured. We are also a lot better at diagnosing cancer now. Death records in the past included causes like "heartbreak," "suddenness," "found dead in street," "stomach pains," and etc.', "Well, Cancer is what gets you when nothing else gets you. To quote another redditor. Before it really was understood, people assumed the issues were caused by another disease. Only'recently' we have learned to rule other diseases out better.,So, basically everyone needs to die from something. In a Health Services Research course that I took last semester, my professor discussed this in detail. We've managed to find ways to treat heart disease and respiratory ailmentsinfections. Cancer is a tougher nut to crack. Here's a link to the [CDC website that has 75 years of mortality in the US by cause] (URL0). You'll note that we've made progress in a lot of areas, but cancer is relatively stable. Because of that, more people die from it because they aren't dieing from other things. Diagnostics have also gotten better at finding cancer sooner. This means that people might know they have extremely early stage tumors years before symptoms start. In the past, you knew you had cancer for maybe a year and then you just died. Now people can have a cancer diagnosis for years. TL;DR: Valar Morghulis, we're just better at other things, and we can detect it earlier now so people "have cancer" longer.', "Cancer is, by and large, an old person's disease. In order for cancer to be a major factor, the population has to live long enough to get it. So, one key reason that cancer has become more prevalent is because people are living longer. There are also other environmental concerns.,I think you got your answer here, but I want to sum it up as I have heard it: cancer is what kills you when everything else has failed. There is always a risk of cancer, and the longer you live, the more opportunities the universe has to screw up your DNA in just the right way that your cells start growing out of control. People are less likely to be killed by malaria and polio and the flu, so they are surviving long enough to lose to cancer.', "Life style choices also play a large part in this. For example links can be made between smoking, drinking and obesity as causes of cancer. Cancer research also suggests that it is said lifestyle choices that make white women as the highest risk ethnicity to develop breast cancer. However, some cancers develop in people who do not smoke or drink so I can't argue that these factors are the sole cause of cancer at all.," "Not to be the hippie of the thread, but I do think we introduce way more carcinogens into our bodies now than we used to. The chemicals that go into food, clothing, body care products, etc. are probably a big factor. (If it was just an age thing then we wouldn't be having twenty year olds and fifty year olds as the common age dying; living to fifty isn't that new by health standards).,more people visiting doctors early, fewer people just sucking it up and living with the problems caused by cancer

article: Think of entropy as chaos. Disorder. If I took a pack of cards, there's only one way the pack can be entirely in order, so the entropy is low. If I shuffle it a little bit, the entropy increases, and it increases more the more I shuffle it - that is, there are lots of possible ways for the cards to be arranged, so the entropy is high. This is also why your room seems to get messier; a chaotic room is entropically favoured over a tidy, ordered room. It's why your headphones always seem to tangle themselves in your pocket - they can only be tidy one way, and massively tangled in potentially billions of ways. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a system will spontaneously increase. Spontaneously here means'without someone giving it a helping hand'. Your room can return to a lower entropic state, if you put energy into tidying it. You can untangle your headphones, but this takes energy. A slightly more advanced example is that solids have a lower entropy than liquid, as the atoms are all stuck in place, as opposed to liquids where the atoms can flow around one another, like balls in a ball pit. Obviously, gases have a higher entropy still. TL,DR: Entropy is disorder.,Have you ever built a house of cards? You start stacking cards on top of each other, one by one, slowly increasing the size of the structure. It takes you a lot of time and energy, but you finally finish. Just as you are about to take a picture, your little brother comes in and knocks it over. The structure that took you hours to build is destroyed in a matter of seconds. This is entropy- energy must be spent to create order from chaos, and since chaos is easier to maintain than order, things tend towards chaos.', "1st Law of Thermo: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. 2nd Law of Thermo: Entropy So lets say you drop a dictionary. It falls, hits the ground, and stops. When it was falling, it had kinetic energy. When it stops, that energy must have gone somewhere, and it goes into heat and sound. But why can't the reverse happen? Why can't I heat up the floor a smidge, set a dictionary on the floor, yell at it, and have the dictionary fly up into the air? That's entropy. Entropy says that the kinetic energy that the dictionary had is happier being heat and sound, so it won't go back into moving the dictionary.,Entropy is a measure of ignorance. Suppose you have a system with N possible states. You know that it is in state number 7. The probability that it is in state number 7 is 1; the probability that it is in any other state is 0. The entropy is 0. Some time later you don't know anything about the state of the system. The probability that the system is in any state is 1N. The entropy is at its maximum. There is a derivation I read in some physics textbook that says that the only formula in concord with the intuitive notion "measure of ignorance" and some reasonable assumptions is: H - S p log p where the summation is done over all the states of the system, and p is the probability of each state.','Brian Cox explained it in a pretty simple way. Hopefully this is viewable to the rest of the world. URL0

article: The Earth is not as hot as it would have to be for this to happen. Radioactive elements in the Earth are decaying at a constant rate. This generates heat. The heat does build up inside the Earth. Magma rises in plumes towards the surface. At points the magma does come out in volcanos as lava. The radioactive elements have been decaying steadily since they were formed in the Supernova which gave rise to our solar system. When the Earth was younger there were probably more volcanos conducting heat away from the center.', "most volcanoes are not caused by internal heat trying to get out, they are caused by ocean plates dragging water under the surface as they plunge underneath continental plates. The water mixes with magma causing it to lose density and become less viscous and start its way up into the continental shelf. In a way, these are all active at the same time, there is something called the ring of fire, all around the pacific plate which is being overrun by surrounding tectonic plates in a process called subduction. There is another subduction zone in the caribbean, another in the mediterranean, and one in the eastern indian ocean. Incidentally, where plates collide it's possible that no subduction takes place, instead we get compression, and this causes mountains to form, as in india-asia and the himalaya. The Alps are a case of there was compression until the african plate started to slip under the eurasian plate and now it's a subduction zone. The Andes are the same story. The rockies were a compression zone until the pacific plate changed direction, and subduction in japan and the rest of asia and alaska is so strong that it's pulling the entire pacific plate north west, turning its eastern border into a slip zone. Plume volcanoes are caused by magma currents inside the mantle, and those are about releasing heat. The thing is, the crust is very bad at keeping heat in, it's just not strong enough, so it's not like heat builds and builds and builds until pressure must be relieved.... The crust is at best like a skin on a cream soup, when the liquid below boils through the bubbles are quite able to pierce the surface without problem. But there is also tremendous heat at the core, below the mantle. This heat is very much contained sometimes, and the result when this is released is a core plume that can cause a huge mind shattering volcanic event. To give you a sense of scale: such a plume in the Deccan traps in india caused an eruption that laid down 2 km thick of magma in just one or two millions years on an area twice the size of texas. Another older event in siberia released up to 4 times as much magma. (these events were so tremendous their ages correlate to to huge mass extinction events, which is not a coincidence.),Short answer is gravity. Magmalava is heavy! Lava gets "shot out" of the earth when enough pressure builds up behind it. But that's got to be a lot of pressure, and usually there isn't enough.','Think of it like a pot of water, it bubbles up in small amounts across the pot, but not as one giant bubble', "Volcanoes aren't'connected'. Hot spots create magma pockets in different places at differing rates of build up.

article: They reference gear ratios. 2.0 would indicate gearing that halves the speed. So if the engine is revving at 5000 rpm (revolutions per minute), the tyre will turn at half that (2500). So for your example of 4.1, etc, its just engine revs divided by ratio (4.1, etc) and that's how fast the wheels turn. To visualise the difference imagine a giant cog, spinning a really small cog. The big one spins once, while the small one spins 4.1 times. The engine is the small one, since its easier to spin something small. Now it's not quite as simple as that, since each gear has a different ratio (a higher number means its easier to turn the wheels), and then the differentials (the big round bit in between the 2 wheels) also have a ratio.

article: 1. They know where the sticky parts are. Spiders can produce many different types of silk, and most of it is not sticky. Typically, only the spiral part of the web is sticky, and the spokes are non-sticky. 2. article: It probably sounds worse than it really is for the speakers. There are a few types of distortion in audio but when it comes to loud volumes causing distortion, that's called clipping. In the audio electrical circuit, there is "clean headroom" up to a certain volume. Let's say the input audio is 2 volts AC peak to peak. The amplifier circuit has up to 10 V peak to peak of clean headroom. If you turn up the gain (via the volume knob) to a 10x gain, it will clip causing distortion. Even though the input was 2V and the gain was 10x, the output will only be slightly higher than 10 V, (probably a bit below 11 V) but it will sound very distorted. As long as the cell phone manufacturer paired a speaker that can handle the maximum output of the integrated amplifier, your cell phone speaker will be fine. The cell phone manufacturer may have even intentionally designed clipping to limit the output. In other amplifier speaker setups like guitars and home stereo, that is where it can be a problem. Many things need to be considered for pairing a speaker and amplifier. Home hi-fi, PA setups, and guitarbass amps all have very high clean headroom (lots of volts of potential gain) so the total amplification can be very high and clipping is usually not intentionally used to limit the output (except for guitar some guitar amps settings and cheap home stereos). In addition to the voltage amplifier that multiplies the voltage, they have large power amplifiers that increase the current output to drive the large speakers. Which is a very different design from the cell phones because they have a buffer circuit drive the speaker rather than a power amplifier. the buffer just matches the impedence to the little speaker but doesn't really increase the wattage very much because it's such a small speaker. With some amplifiers the output goes through a transformer. If the speaker and transformer do not have matched impedences, the transformer can burn out and damage the rest of the amplifier. If the speakers cannot handle the total output in watts of the amplifier, the speakers coil can burnout. In vintage speakers, the cone could rip. Also if a bass guitar amp is used on a vintage or cheap guitar speaker cabinet, the cone could rip. In modern (past 20 years or so) decent quality speakers, the speakers will be fine but the sound would distort and sound farty. Make sure the speakers have the same impedence as needed by the amplifier. Make sure the wattage of the speakers exceeds the wattage of the amplifier. Speakers are often advertised with its peak ratings. You need to match the RMS wattages of the speaker and amp. Don't use peak watts when pairing speakers with an amp. For good sound, make sure you use the right type of speaker with the amplifier. Use hi-fi speakers with hi-fi amps. Use guitar speakers for guitar amps. Use similar wattage ratings: if it's a 100W amp, use a 100W speaker. If possible, buy a matched set of speakers and amps of the same brand and series. The manufacturer probably matched the amp and speakers for a reason.

article: Both have to do with chemical imbalances in the brain. What you're talking about has a clinical term called "Anhedonia" which is the inability to feel pleasure and is an actual clinical symptom and diagnosis. The big one in depression is the lack of serotonin. Serotonin helps us feel hungry when we are, helps us sleep when we're tired, helps us regulate our mood, and inhibits some pain (Cymbalta is marketed to help with this). If your body knows it's tired and hungry, it's not going to want to do anything until those physiological needs are taken care of (Think Maslow's hierarchy of needs). The other big one is dopamine, which is often regarded as part of the brain's reward system. This is why people with PSA (poly-substance abuse) often seek drugs. It releases dopamine. However with depression dopamine at a reduced level. No reward means no action. One of the biggest thing someone with depression can do is to exercise. Study shows it helps. I'm no expert, but just took a class which covered some of this, but it's really amazing what the brain does, and experts will tell you a lot of what the medical field does, they don't know the mechanism of action, but they just know "it works.,'To be honest, exercise truly does help. That is one thing I would share with others as well','There's no single theory that is accepted for mood disorders. But there are a lot of parts that you can take together to explain it. From a neuropsychological perspective, depression has its effect on two main areas. The first is the area at the forefront of your brain, behind your forehead. The Prefrontal Cortex or PFC. The second is the limbic system, a somewhat deep rooted connected series of structures that sit below your walnut-like hemispheres. The PFC is what makes you who you are. Your personality, motivation, drive and internal goals all come from here. The limbic system is what regulates your emotions. How you feel, what you fear and love, how you recall emotions and emotionally react to everything is based in here. The neuropsych aspect looks at the interplay between these two structures. Think of your mood as being a tug of war between these two players, and the way you are as a person is determined by which brain circuit is more active. Others look at the monoamine hypothesis, which suggests that mood disorders are simply a result of transmitter imbalance in these areas. Which is why drugs are used to effect a change and control the problem. In either case, emotions have an effect on internal motivation. You could argue that most humans, even the most logical ones, do things out of an emotional core or drive. Depression isn't just unhappiness. It's numbness. It's pervasive sadness and a LACK of satisfaction and joy. Most depressed people have a hard time feeling motivated due to this imbalance, and in most cases, the negative mood that comes with it also impacts the motivation and drive of the person suffering. So it becomes a bad cycle, "You're in a bad mood, but you don't want to do anything, so your mood worsens and leaves you more incapacitated." Not everybody reaches this stage. If you look at depression as a spectrum, the key is to get help quickly. If you're slightly more mindful or have recovered from an episode, you can get out of it by doing things to automatically boost your mood. Like the peaceful high from a nice run or exercise, natural endorphins work really well for that. You said that you've been diagnosed with a bipolar mood disorder. So you would had to have had a moment where your mood was pretty high. You might have noticed that you'd have been extremely motivated, productive and even prodigous at your work. It's the same deal. TL;DR The brain circuits that control your emotion experience faulty transmission, and that affects your mood, which also affects your drive and motivation. These brain circuits interact with each other and effectively pull each other down. The same happens in mania, but in the opposite direction. Essentially, it boils down to this: Emotion affects your motivation, and your actions will have an impact on your emotions.', "As I understand it, depression is a loss of interest and a lot of times a loss of drive. Depression can't just be flipped off, obviously, with most psychological problems. As well, the things that used to make you happy (sports, hobbies, meeting and interacting with people) simply don't anymore. The unhappiness partially stems from whatever is causing the depression, be it hormones, brain chemistry, or actual physiological differences, and from the fact that you don't get the joy from the things that used to make you happy. It's very difficult to fix depression by yourself without the assistance of medicine or psychological counseling. However, if you could, it'd be very hard because you're not inspired to do that. Think about it like if you're lazy (not relevant to depression, just a regular lazy person). There's literally only one way to cure laziness: stop being lazy. However, it's directly counterintutitive to what laziness is; you have to be able to cure the thing that's ailing you by not being it which doesn't just happen (except through willpower with laziness but you're generally pretty low on that if you're lazy). It's similar with depression.... The only way to stop being depressed is to stop being depressed but how are you going to stop being depressed while you're depressed? There are a number of steps you can take to work through or manage depression and its symptoms the same way with somebody who's lazy (they can set goals, give themselves motivation, and learn methods to combat it). However, something like that is outside of your own mentalemotional control and therefore is very difficult to consciously fix.
