article: I believe it's mostly about efficiency. It takes a lot of time and energy to give every citizen in a society a voice in decision-making. Having one person, or a small group, take responsibility for all decisions is fast and effective, as is replacing those people when they make mistakes. Consensus-based organizations, where everyone has to agree on each decision, are horribly slow to move or change (look at any community-focused non profit), where corporations, for all their evil, are fast to adapt and implement new strategies (even if the new strategies are stupid and hurt the business).,Because power doesn't lie with the people but with the army. Even in an 'absolute monarchy', the nobility would exercise a large amount of authority - the monarch would have the final word, but if they tried to simply overrule the majority of the nobility, they'd find themselves facing a revolution. What we view as 'democracy' only comes into being when the class of people whose opinion actually matters expands dramatically - generally either due to the community being small and tight-knit or the rise of a professional middle class. It's simply too cumbersome to do backroom politicking with everyone whose voice is relevant to the process, so you create a voting system. Note that in the absence of the conditions necessary for democracy, you can still vote. article: NLY5] Lots of sites are using it at least a little. You wouldn't necessarily know it to see it though. In HTML4, if you wanted a video, you had to reach for Flash or Silverlight and embed the video in a site with code (think about the old cut-and-paste stuff to embed content that YouTube would provide). In HTML5, there are audio and video elements integrated into the language - no external plugins required. There's drag-and-drop capability (like how you can drag and drop a file into SkyDrive in your browser, or the way gmail has integrated drag-and-drop), so there's more interaction programmed in. There's also a move towards offline stuff. For example, you could write something in Office365 or GoogleDocs even with no internet connection and then it would sync the next time you're online.,This is a bit of a complex question so I'll answer it as best I can. New "semantic" tags HTML5 is the next step in creating a more "semantic web," meaning that browsers can more easily tell what format certain data is in. In the past, web pages have been structured using something called "divs" (which, in code is the div tag). In order to differentiate them, most coders use an attribute within the div tag, known as "id" or "class." This is like giving a label to that div so it's known by a specific name or group. (For example: if I have a div that will serve as the header of my page, I might use the tag div id"header" .) This is all fine and well, but when a browser reads this code, it can't understand that this specific div is meant to be the header of the page. It just knows that it's called "header." In HTML5, there is actually a tag now called header . This adds "semantic value," or meaning, to the tag itself, meaning that it's easier for a browser that reads the code to know that this section is the header of a page. So, why is that important? It's for the sake of search engines like Google, who can filter through certain parts of a page when you're looking for something and improve the quality and the accuracy of your search results, making it easier for you to find what you're looking for. This same concept applies to a lot of other elements of the page. Instead of using a generic object tag that could be one of many things (images, audio, video, Flash, etc.), you can now use semantic tags called video or audio . So, instead of the browser reading the code and saying "okay, this is an object, now what type is it?," it will say "okay, this is clearly a video." The canvas tag Think about all of the fancy animations and such that Flash webpages are able to do. The canvas tag will allow web designersdevelopers to achieve many of those same effects using just HTML and JavaScript code (JavaScript being another powerful web language that works with HTML to create complex actions and applications) instead of needing to use Flash, which can be slow to load and bandwidth-heavy. Why is this a good thing? It simplifies the process of designing rich graphics and interactive elements without needing to learn and resort to a third-party technology like Flash. It's also more portable and scalable to mobile browsing, whereas Flash has had well-documented problems making the jump to smartphones. Application caching Ever been doing something on a webpage (like using an application or filling out a form) and your internet connection went out, so you lose your data and can't finish what you were doing? HTML5 solves that problem by using what's called "application caching." Basically, when the browser reads the code and comes across a tag that looks like this: html manifest"filename.manifest" .... it will read the manifest file to figure out what files a specific webapp needs to run. It will then download them and store them on your computer so that if you need to use the webapp offline, it will still function. Why is this a good thing? Obviously, it allows for a lot more flexibility in terms of how webapps are used. If you're on the go and you can't get WiFi or 3G coverage, you can still use those webapps to accomplish various things without needing an internet connection. Those are just a couple of reasons, but they're what I'd call the major ones. It's really about helping code writers write cleaner, simpler and less code, while improving HTML's capabilities and organizing data better so it's easier to sort and find. HTML5 is still in development and isn't scheduled to be finalized until around 2022, but many of its abilities are already being implemented into more progressive webpages. The drawback is that browsers don't have full capability to understand everything that HTML5 tries to do, so some of it breaks. When you're designing a webpage, you need to consider "cross-browser compatibility," meaning that you make sure the page will look the same and work the same, no matter what browser or version someone is using. Internet Explorer 6 is notoriously bad for developers because it doesn't support many of the newer features and many people (usually older people or non-computer savvy people) don't understand the importance of upgrading their browser, so web developers will need to cater to the lowest common denominator in many cases. Hope this explanation helps. I didn't cover everything, but maybe this will explain the general reason why HTML5 is a "big deal.,Facetheduke] (URL0) explains it pretty well. article: from [Iowa ENT Center] (URL0) What is a turbinate? A turbinate is a strip of tissue along the lining of the nose. It can swell or shrink based on many factors. When swollen, it blocks airflow; when decongested, it permits airflow. The turbinate is responsible for the back-and-forth nasal blockage people experience. For instance, when one rolls over in bed and one side of the nose opens and the other closes off, it is the turbinate swelling on one side and shrinking on the other that is responsible for this change.', "when sick? I've always only been able to breath our of one nostril: (it changes from time to time.," "I get this too, especially at the moment due to my cold. It's not due to any actual mucus that you feel you have a blocked nose, it's actually an infection swelling your blood vessels in your nose that causes the blockage. When you lie on your side with a blocked nose, the blood in the vessels have weight and do shift, albeit ever so slightly, from one side of the nostril to the other. This means that although it feels like you have something in your nose, it's actually the nostril's passage that is being changed in shape and size.,When you're sick and your nose is stopped up, it's actually not from mucoussnot, it's from inflammation in the lining of your nose. As the lining fills with blood, it swells, blocking your nasal passage. Rolling from one side to the other affects how the blood drains. When you roll over what you find is that the "higher" side of your nose is the part you can breathe out of...It is actually physically harder for your heart to pump to the higher side, and it's easier for the blood to drain back, so the inflammation isn't so bad. Something to notice is that when you cry, your nasal passage isn't inflamed in the same way it is when you're fighting an infection. You actually produce a tremendous amount of mucous when you cry, but you can easily blow it out and breathe freely. TL;DR, Stuffed up feeling isn't from snot, it's from nasal passage inflammation, rolling over helps "drain" the blood allows you to breathe again.','Wait, why have I never heard of this? I almost wish I had a blocked nose so I could try it.', "I asked my ENT about this, except it's slightly different. When one of my nostril's is clogged, it will randomly clear up and the other one will get clogged. It will swap back and forth all day, but not as a result of lying down. People are correct that it's the inflamed turbinates, but the question is why does it switch sides? He told me it was actually neurological and that they didn't know the reason it happens.,There's something called a "Nasal Cycle" where which nostril you are primarily breathing through switches. This change occurs every 2-3 hours on average. When you are congested it becomes more obvious which side is which at the given time.

article: The people who design computers make them do lots of clever things to save power when they're running on battery power instead of AC. One of the things they do is run the processor more slowly, so that it uses less power. Just like driving your car at 130 miles per hour on the freeway will use more fuel than driving at 56 miles per hour on the freeway over the same distance, making the processor run slower will also use less power than running it faster. Similar tricks are done with other parts of the computer too, like turning off the hard disk if you don't use it for 30 seconds - spinning the disk inside a hard disk is a huge power drain.," "This is known as [frequency scaling] (URL0) or CPU throttling. The processor allows for separate'levels' of operation in which the frequency is adjusted. Your operating system determines that you are currently running on battery power, so it tries to reduce the energy consumed by lowering the frequency on the processor. When you plug the AC power back in, it bumps the frequency back up. This is done so that the consumer can continue using the laptop for longer. It would be quite annoying if your laptop ran out of power within half an hour. Your OS should also come with the option to avoid this sluggishness when on battery power. You will be able to go into something like'power options' and keep performance up even when on battery power, at the expense of having to recharge sooner. If you are on Windows 7, you can left click the battery icon in your system tray and choose'high performance' when you're on battery mode.

article: Amber and green are both due to differently diluted amounts of melanin in the outer layer of the iris. (If the inner layer is affected, you get reddish albino eyes...) Blue eyes indicate absence of melanin, it is a structure that happens to just scatter the light to appear blue. Similar to blue bird feathers, Morpho butterfly wings, the sky and the sea (Not identical mechanisms) Black eyes are chock full of melanin. Inbetween you have gradients of dilution of melanin, with green being the underlying structural blue with a very slight yellow smattering of melanin, mixing it to appear green; hazel being a bit more, so the warm yellow aspect is stronger, etc. You inherit the instructions for how much melanin (and pheomelanin which is light red) you produce. Your parents have different amounts and versions of the genes carrying these instructions, written into DNA, which is bunched into chromosomes. Humans have usually two sets of chromosomes. During meiosis (when egg cells and sperm cells are created), chromosomes get split up and the DNA untangled, then there's some swapping between corresponding chromosomes with a chance of deletion or duplication, so you get a pretty random half of their genes and some extra variation, too! When an egg and sperm cell unite, there's again some crossing over between the chromosomes the sperm and those the egg brings. And in the end, you get a random mixture of what the parents have in THEIR genes. It can be pretty surprising, one parent might have donated more copies than one of a melanin-producing gene so a child might have a trait as strong as that parent, or get only a fraction of it. (I'm the tanning, blond haired, blue eyed white dragon of a darker-skinned black-haired brown-eyed guy and a green-eyed, very pale and sunburning mother because my dad had an extra copy of "no melanin, please" lying around that I got, but was overshadowed in him by his melanin-producing genes) All this means that you can approximately, but never with 100 certainty calculate the odds of producing offspring with a certain eye and skin color. (Skin color is also partly linked to the sex chromosome X.) ', "There are some traits that blend, rather than select one or the other. Which traits do this seems to vary from one species to another. One example is coat coloring in one breed of cows. I gather that farmers noticed that when white cows and brown cows mated, their calves were sometimes white with brown spots. I apologize for lack of detail, since I haven't had a biology focused education since high school, and this was just a factoid I remembered from that class.

article: Ideally, subsidies exist to incentivize behavior which the market doesn't value enough, like development of solar technology or new medical treatments. However, in our country, the biggest recievers of subsidies are oil companies. This is due to corruption.," "We don't have a free market. Humanity hasn't had a free market in the past several hundred years (maybe longer). Corporations need subsidies to compete with other corporations that are receiving direct or indirect subsidies from one or more governments, to balance out trade barriers imposed by other governments, to compensate for the cost of government mandates on how they run their business, etc. None of which is to say that a free market works well - or that it doesn't - it's to say that condemning the free market based on the current system of any nation in the world is baseless.,For farmers at least, the subsidies for crop diversity. Otherwise the farmers would just grow the most profitable crops and nothing else.', "Because the free market is good for the consumer - not for the producer. Especially if you achieve some dominant position in the market and don't want all that pesky competition trying to push you out. It's a story as old as time. You set up a company, want to get a share of the market so you love the free market, want as little regulation as possible and as little taxation as possible because you work your ass off and want all the fruits of your labour. In time you grow in size, acquire and stabilize your market share and suddenly you don't want to work as hard as before. You want to live the good life, spend, use the wealth for pleasure rather than for constant battle with young or innovative competitors. So you start promoting regulation - to equalize the playing field..so that only approved things are allowed. No tricks. You start promoting taxes because rich can't be greedy.... but it just so happens that outsourcing profits is also easier for you - a big corporation - than your sole owner competitor in a garage. You opt for subsidies because they are allocated according to rules set by politicians - which again benefit you - not the competitors. In other words... capitalism for the poor but socialism for the rich.... since the dawn of time.," "Subsidies come when the government doesn't want the free market to work. The free market may cause your country to be uncompetitive in an industry, and that industry would shut down in a free market. The government would then decide to subsidize that industry to keep them afloat and keep those jobs and voters. Government intervention is an attempt to interfere with the free market for some political or nationalistic reason.," "They don't, and corporations getting in bed with the government has nothing to do with free market values. That's corporatism, something free market advocates acknowledge is an abuse of capitalism and something that should be prevented.," "The question doesn't really make much sense. Obviously it's not a truly free market if companies are getting government subsidies. In a completely free market that corporation would collapse and be replaced by more competentcheaper competitors. Government intervention (also known as the opposite of a free market) keeps these corporations afloat for a variety of reasons. They either believe that the collapse of that corporation will have far reaching negative consequences on the economy as a whole (like why they bailed out banks), or they believe that it provides a service that is beneficial but there isn't much of a market for (like government art grants).," "A pure free market only works if you make certain assumptions. 1. Everyone is completely rational 2. The market is highly competitive- everything is created and sold by multiple companies. 3. Everyone has access to all the information they need to make those perfectly rational decisions. 4. The short term doesn't really matter, only the long term. 2 and 4 are the bigger problems when it comes to subsidies, 3 is important when it comes to regulations, and 1 sort of balances itself out in the long run. The problem with 2 is that there's a lot of research into new technologies that goes on these days. The technology undoubtably is a good thing from an economic perspective- it lets us make more stuff with less other stuff. But doing the actual research is expensive, and no one is going to fund research if everyone else can take their ideas and make it themselves. Those copycats get all the benefits of the new tech and none of the costs. The problem with 4 is that when all of your farmers are growing corn because it's the most profitable crop, and then there's a disease that wipes out all the corn, you're left with a bunch of starving farmers and a population that now doesn't have enough food. Sure in the long run it will work out, but you need to have that diversity and a safety net just in case for the short term. The problem with 3 is that the company knows way more about the product than you do. In our theoretical perfect market, snake oil salesmen would never make a sale because everyone would know that it's just snake oil. Also in our theoretical perfect market, you'd know all about the reliability of your car, and how long you'll get to use your new computer before it breaks. You also don't know how much the medical bills are going to cost when you develop lung problems from all the pollution the factories are dumping into the air and when you get sick from the toxins they're dumping into the water supply. These are negative externalities- costs to society that, without perfectly rational actors in a society with perfect information, won't be reflected in the cost of the goods. So there are government regulations on what they have to tell you and what they have to do to ensure the products are safe and live up to the claims they make, as well as a carrot- subsidies for doing things that are beneficial to society even if they won't immediately be able to make up the cost of cutting pollution or whatever.," "The free marketer point of view would be that they aren't needed and America is poorer because they get them. They exist because it is extremely beneficial for a company to pursue them. Think of it this way: if you owned a business would you rather get 0 from the government or 100million? You could spend a lot lobbying for that 100million and still come out ahead. Various reports have found the return on investment for lobbying for subsidies is over 10,000. Subsidies can come to exist for other reasons too. In some districts that are heavily invested in one industry (eg farming) people will vote for candidates who get more subsidies because while it is bad for the economy as a whole it is good for the people in that district. Of course if businesses and politicians call it what it is, crony capitalism, voters would probably get upset. But if they spin it as a necessary part of the capitalist system then people seemingly accept that answer.

article: Matter (in the everyday sense) is made of molecules, which are made of atoms, which are made of particles: protons, neutrons and electrons. That seemed to be the whole story, and that the component particles of atoms were "fundamental" - they weren't made of anything else, they were just kind of themselves. But then we found out that protons and neutrons are actually made of smaller particles, which are called "quarks." Quarks have some interesting properties. It turns out that quarks have six different "flavors" just intrinsically different varieties. There are only a handful of stable combinations of flavors that will last when they clump together. Other combos break down quickly or never form at all. And most importantly and weirdly, they can't be separated - they can only exist in these combos. Particles made of combinations of quarks are called, as a family, "hadrons." The protons and neutrons we know so well from our daily lives are the most stable combination of quarks, which are made of just two flavors called "up" and "down" quarks. These are also the most stable flavors of quarks - other flavors quickly decay into up and downs. But there are also more exotic combinations of quarks that show up as relatively short-lived particles in cosmic rays and stuff. These can involve combinations of the other four flavors of quark: "strange," "charm," "bottom," and "top." Quarks and hadrons have a lot of other interesting properties and important roles in particle physics. But to everyday human experience, the combos of up and down quarks that we know as protons and neutrons are the biggest part of the picture.','The bartender on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine.','Related: Please explain how a quark and a neutrino are related, if at all.

article: The rule about "no metal in the microwave" is actually one that exists more for the sake of simplicity. It isn't a hard and fast rule of science. There are times when it's okay to have metal in the microwave. Metals reflect most of the microwave energy, which is why the microwave oven itself is made of metal to keep the radiation inside the microwave oven. A metal bowl, in general, is okay to put in the microwave, provided that it's completely smooth and doesn't ever touch the walls of the microwave. It just reflects radiation around in the oven, but doesn't have any sharp prongs to create electrical arcs with. Food products like Hot Pockets have metallic cages that can be used to reflect microwave radiation in a certain way that cooks the food in a desirable way. Whatever metal items come inside the microwave are either designed in a way that won't create arcs, or perhaps, they're made of metal alloys that don't interact much with the radiation. Such alloys do exist.','A lot of microwaveable food comes with some sort of metallic heating shroud in it to help cook better. Then danger is when you put something in that has the right shape and topography to be able to arc. If you put a spoon in the microwave, your microwave will be ok, and the spoon will heat. If you put a fork in, you will get arc between the tines. Those sparks arcing around are what can be harmful to the microwave.', "The top comments are correct, but they don't mention this very simple rule of thumb: sharp angles more likely to spark. In general, anything metal with sharp angles (fork, aluminum foil, etc) is probably a bad idea to microwave. Smooth metal, not so much.

article: I work as a psych nurse and can answer part of your question. If the person has mental illness and meets criteria for detainment (they pose a danger to themselves or others or are so psychotic they can't make decisions for themselves), then a mental health officer could be called and place the person under an emergency detention. A psych hospital can accept the person as a patient and keep them up to 72 hours for treatment. A lot of homeless people brought in on EDs don't have IDs. We just take their word for it as to what their name is. We had a psychotic person come in once under one name, got treated, discharged, stopped taking her meds, became psychotic again, and came back under a different name. Admissions didn't catch it, but we did once she got to the unit, so we changed it back to her original name just to keep all her records congruent. But honestly, we had no way of knowing which name was the correct one. She came in with nothing but the clothes on her back and 35 cents. That's living free, no ties to anything.," " What happens when someone, like say a homeless person, gets arrested on the streets but has no form of ID on them? The police decide if the name provided is credible, and check if they have that information on record. If they don't, they will create a new record going forward. And say the person has a mental illness and doesn't even know hisher own name? If no name is provider, they make an effort to ID the person by other means. If that doesn't work, the create a John Doe record for them.,Most large jails use a Master Name Index (MNI) to attach all the aliases a person gives to their true identity. As stated before, everyone is fingerprinted to match you to a known person (if you have been fingerprinted in say the last 15 years or so for anything including security clearances, government jobs, previous arrests, etc.) If there is no match, then the arrestee is created as a new record. From there everyone is processed the same - booked, ran through medical, property taken, classified and housed in a cell. Honestly, the detention staff do not care what an aresstee's real name is. They just have to make sure the person brought in is tracked throughout their "stay." Fun interesting side note for homeless - A lot of the time homeless are brought in for trespassing or warrant for failure to appear in court. If arrested for trespassing, they are usually booked and released to show up in court at a specified date and time that will be mailed to them. Since they are homeless and usually not able to receive mail, they never know when to go to court. So they are issued a warrant for not showing up and the endless cycle begins.', "This is a complicated question that varies not only by country, but I Canada varies by province due to the diffetent provincial health acts surrounding mental health. For the most part, in Canada at least, a person can be detained until their identity is discovered. In the case of mentally I'll individuals who are unable to even provide such information they will usually be either known to police from a last encounter or in a facility that would notice their absense. In the later case, the persons identity would be on file from the facility. If the person is not know by either source and they are so mentally unstable that they cannot identify themselves they would most likely be held for their own safetycontinuance. If someone is unable to even tell you thier name they most likely can not survive without assistance anyways.

article: When you connect the two batteries together, does it close a circuit and create one giant battery? Essentially, yes, although the dead battery doesn't contribute much, the live battery is doing all the work. And when dead car starts, is it just drawing power from the giant battery? On the car's motor is running, it is driving the alternator, which charges the battery. Let it run for 10, 15 minutes, and it should have enough juice to start up again.,Sounds like someone is preparing for the Canadian winters.','When you connect the jumper cables between the batteries, you do indeed create one larger battery by connecting the batteries in parallel. But, the battery in the dead car is drained, so only the battery in the other car will contribute when starting. As soon as you connect the cables, the generator in the running car will start to charge the battery in the dead car. Depending a lot on the quality of the jumper cables, you can either start the dead car straight off of the other cars battery. If that doesn't work, you're most likely using low quality cables that have too great of a resistance, which creates a voltage loss when a current is drawn, not being able to provide enough power to the starting car. In that case, just let the "other car" run for 10 minutes (with elevated idling, around rpm is good) while connected, and it's alternator will charge the battery in the dead car. It won't be fully charged in 10 minutes, but because it has charged a bit, less current has to be drawn through the jumper cables since the starter can now use current from that battery too. Less current also means less voltage drop over the cables, providing even more power. So why won't low quality cables allow you to jump start a car directly without charging first? It's because the wires are so thin, and connected so poorly, that the cable has a quite high resistance. Since VIR, higher resistance equals higher voltage loss. When buying jumper cables, always buy the best quality you can find. You can also always double up cables. It's much better to have two pairs of low quality cables connected, than just one pair. Also, when connecting jumper cables, always make sure the clamps get as good of a connection as possible! This is very important, this frequently makes the difference between a successful and unsuccessful jump start. This means, don't just clamp them on and leave them, but pry the handles apart (so the clamps clamp with more force) and rotate the clamp back and forth a bit so it "digs in" a little bit. Sometimes it's necessary to actually have someone holding the cables, he should then try to pry the handles on the jumper cables apart, so they exert more force and "digs in" harder in the metal.

article: The MTHFR gene has the instructions for the body to build an enzyme with a really long name. An enzyme is a protein that helps the body perform chemical reactions. This particular enzyme helps make methionine, one of the building blocks of proteins, and helps the body to use vitamin B9 (also known as folic acid). A genetic mutation is when the gene's instructions are different from that of the regular version of the gene. In other words, the instructions are misspelled. Mutated genes often cause the body to make less effective versions of the corresponding protein. In MTHFR's case, this means that the body produces enzymes that aren't great at making methionine and utilizing vitamin B9. There are multiple medical problems that can result from MTHFR mutations, including increased risk of blood clots and birth defects of the nervous system.

article: 0 of the Fed is under private control. The Fed uses its own set of terminology in which it uses words in a manner that is totally inconsistent with those words' dictionary definitions. For example, the Fed uses words like "stock holder" to refer to a non-ownership relationship that it has with banks. In short, interstate banks are required to deposit money with the Fed. Once this money is deposited, they share data on banking conditions and the monetary supply with the Fed, which then shares that data with other banks. That is the extent of a bank's relationship with the Fed - that of a legally compelled depositor. Its not advisable to try to pick apart the Fed's operations as a layperson. When the Fed came into existence in the early 1900's it was incredibly controversial. To get around this controversy they created a very obtuse system that was design to look like a private bank from the outside. So technically the Fed is composed of multiple banks, each of which have their own "governing" structure. But none of that structure matters because its powerless to act. The only entity with any decision making ability in the Fed is the national Board of Governors, which is appointed entirely by the US Government. Or to put it another way, when the Fed was originally created the idea of the Federal Government being allowed to interfere with the banking system was wildly unpopular. So the original creators of the Fed designed it to look like a private bank that was owned by other private banks to a person who wasn't already familiar with how it works. As unsatisfying as it is, its not possible to explain the intricacies of how the Fed works in a few paragraphs on the internet. If you want an in-depth explanation of it that's something that you basically have to go to school for. Alternatively you can just take it on faith that the regional banks are not actually independent entities and that their governing boards have no actual power or authority.
